ranges.en: Mishna permits irrigating from new or established springs on Festival and Sabbatical, but not from rain cisterns or shaduf water
Circular ditches around vine bases are prohibited on Festival intermediate days
R. Elazar ben Azarya forbids building new water channels on Festival intermediate days or in the Sabbatical year
The Sages permit building a new water channel in the Sabbatical year
The Sages permit repairing damaged water channels on Festival intermediate days
Public-need repairs permitted on Festival days: communal cisterns, roads, streets, ritual baths and other public needs
Marking graves and uprooting prohibited kilayim shoots are also permitted on Festival intermediate days
If irrigation from a newly emerged spring is permitted, why state that an established spring is also permitted?
Had only the new spring been taught, one might infer rain-fed fields may not be watered from established springs; the second case is needed
New and established springs are equivalent: both allowed for fields needing irrigation, neither for rain-fed fields
How do we know that the term beit hashelah denotes thirst or need for water?
Deuteronomy 25:18 uses the word faint, and its Targum renders it as thirsty, supporting the sense of thirst
How do we know that beit haba'al denotes a settled field that needs no extensive upkeep?
Isaiah 62:5 and its Aramaic rendering use settling-down language, supporting the sense of settled
Which anonymous tanna allows loss-preventing labor on Festival days but forbids profit-seeking labor, even when exertion is excessive?
Rav Huna says the Mishna follows R. Eliezer ben Ya'akov
Quotes R. Eliezer ben Ya'akov's mishna: water may be drawn tree to tree, but not the entire field
Perhaps R. Eliezer ben Ya'akov prohibits only profit-seeking labor, and never forbade excessive exertion for loss
Rav Pappa says the Mishna follows the opinion of R. Yehuda
Baraita: R. Meir allows watering rain-fed fields from a new spring; R. Yehuda limits this to fields that dried up
R. Elazar ben Azarya rejects both positions: neither view is correct
R. Yehuda: one may not divert a water channel to water a garden or ruin during Festival intermediate days
What does R. Yehuda mean by a dried-up field? If it is literally dry, why water it?
Abaye: the field's original spring dried up, and a new spring emerged that must be used or the field is ruined
Explains R. Elazar's clause: whether or not the spring dried up makes no difference, and a new spring is not used
Asks how we know the Mishna reflects R. Yehuda: perhaps he permits only new springs, as the Mishna's first clause states

ranges.en: A spring that did not just emerge is stable, so even a rain-fed field may be irrigated from it
If so, which tanna is the Mishna attributed to?
Rather, it follows R. Yehuda: no difference between springs; irrigation allowed only for fields needing it
The baraita stated the new-spring case to convey R. Meir's broader view, permitting even rain-fed fields
For which prohibited labor on Shabbat are we obligated to forewarn one who weeds or waters seedlings?
Rabba: the forewarning is for the prohibition of plowing
Rav Yosef: the forewarning is for the prohibition of sowing
Rabba's rationale: weeding loosens the soil as plowing does, so it matches plowing
Rav Yosef's rationale: watering makes the fruit grow as sowing does, so it matches sowing
Abaye: each view is difficult, since weeding and watering must fall under both plowing and sowing
If one holds that an action falls under only one category, the Gemara objects from a known ruling
Rav Kahana: pruning vines on Shabbat for wood creates liability for both sowing and reaping
The difficulty stands on both opinions
Rav Yosef objects with a baraita: weeding near diverse kinds is flogged, which Rabba's view cannot explain
The baraita continues with R. Akiva: even maintaining a mixture of kinds is flogged
Rav Yosef: on my view, weeding is sowing, so flogging is explained; on yours, plowing involves no mixture
Rabba: the flogging is for maintaining a mixture of kinds, not for plowing
The anonymous first tanna must then hold flogging is for some other labor, since R. Akiva's clause is separate
The whole baraita is R. Akiva's view, so the objection fails
What is the reason the baraita gives for flogging weeders who handle diverse kinds?
The reason given: weeding and covering diverse kinds is flogged for maintaining the mixture, per R. Akiva
What is the reason for R. Akiva's opinion, and how did he derive it from the verses?
Leviticus 19:19: your field shall not be sown with mingled seed
The verse limits the prohibition to sowing, so where is maintaining a mixture derived?
Reading the verse with a different punctuation yields that maintaining diverse kinds in one's field is prohibited
The Mishna taught that one may irrigate on Festival intermediate days and in the Sabbatical year
On the Festival, loss permits exertion; but is the Sabbatical different?
Are sowing and plowing permitted in the Sabbatical year when the Torah explicitly prohibits them?
Abaye: the Mishna refers to the present Sabbatical, a rabbinic obligation, and follows R. Yehuda HaNasi
Baraita: R. Yehuda HaNasi reads Deuteronomy 15:2 as two releases, land and money
The verse equates the two releases, so land release is not Torah-mandated now, only rabbinic
Rava: even per the Rabbis, the leniency applies because only primary categories of labor are Torah-prohibited

ranges.en: The Torah prohibited only the principal categories of Sabbatical labor; derivative subcategories are not Torah-prohibited
Leviticus 25:4 cited: the field shall not be sown and the vineyard not pruned
Since pruning falls under sowing and grape picking under reaping, why did the Torah write them explicitly?
They were enumerated to make only these subcategories flogged-worthy, not other subcategories
Is there really no liability for other subcategories? A baraita asks where weeding and hoeing are derived
The baraita derives weeding and cutting from the repeated wording: no labor in your field or vineyard
From where is it derived that pruning trees and trimming large branches are prohibited?
The same verse wording, read as prohibiting all labor in field and vineyard, answers this
From where is it derived that fertilizing and removing stones or fumigating trees are prohibited?
The same verse wording again covers fertilizing, stone removal, dust-covering roots and fumigation
One might think light hoeing, filling cracks with water and ditches are also prohibited, which would overreach
Therefore the verse states: your field you shall not sow, limiting the prohibition
Sowing is singled out to compare: only labor performed in both field and vineyard is prohibited, not vineyard-only labor
Most of these labors are rabbinic; the verse is only a mnemonic support, not a Torah source
Is light hoeing under olive trees permitted during the Sabbatical year?
Exodus 23:11: let it rest (light hoeing) and lie fallow (clearing stones) indicates hoeing is prohibited
Rav Ukva bar Ḥama: hoeing to strengthen trees is prohibited, but hoeing to seal cracks is permitted
R. Yoḥanan and R. Elazar disagree on whether one who plows in the Sabbatical year is flogged
Perhaps they disagree over R. Avin's principle as stated by R. Ile'a?
R. Avin's principle quoted from R. Ile'a: a general positive command with a negative detail is not expanded to similar cases
The one who says flogged rejects R. Avin's principle, so plowing is derived from the generalization-detail-generalization pattern
The one who says not flogged holds in accordance with R. Avin's ruling, so plowing is not extended from the detail
The Gemara rejects this: everyone agrees R. Avin's principle is not the halakha
According to the one who says flogged, the derivation works well, using the generalization-detail-generalization principle
The one who says not flogged argues that enumerated subcategories alone create liability, so plowing is not included
Isn't it taught in a baraita that weeding and cutting are derived from the verse's wording? From where?
The verse: no labor in your field or vineyard, teaching that all field labor is prohibited
From where is pruning trees and trimming branches derived?
The verse wording covers all labor performed in field and vineyard
From where is fertilizing and removing stones derived?
The same verse covers all labor in field and vineyard, including fertilizing and fumigation
One might think light hoeing and filling cracks are permitted, but the verse suggests otherwise
The verse states: your field you shall not sow, limiting the prohibition to sowing
Sowing is singled out to compare other labors: only those performed in both field and vineyard are prohibited
These labors are prohibited only rabbinically; the verse is a mere support, not a Torah source

ranges.en: Rav Dimi arrives from Eretz Yisrael and relates a tradition he heard there
The tradition: one might be flogged for the addition, but a teaching exempts it from lashes
Rav Dimi says he does not know which teaching or which addition the tradition refers to
R. Elazar: the addition is plowing in the Sabbatical year, which is derived by generalization-detail-generalization but exempt from lashes
Logic: if plowing were flogged, why would the verse enumerate pruning and grape picking? Only these are flogged
R. Yoḥanan: the addition refers to the extra days the Sages added before Rosh HaShana of the Sabbatical year
Plowing and reaping on those extra days are derived from Exodus 34:21 but are exempt from lashes
What are the extra days before Rosh HaShana?
Mishna Shevi'it 1:1: Beit Shammai allow plowing while it benefits the existing fruit; Beit Hillel allow it until Shavuot
Mishna Shevi'it 2:1: a white field may be plowed until the moisture ceases, while people plant cucumbers and gourds
R. Shimon: if no set time was fixed, each person would determine his own time, which the Torah does not allow
R. Shimon sets fixed times: white field until Passover, orchard until Shavuot, and Beit Hillel say Passover
R. Shimon ben Pazi, citing bar Kappara: Rabban Gamliel and his court voted to nullify these restrictions
R. Zeira asks how Rabban Gamliel's court could nullify the decree of Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel, who were greater
Mishna Eduyot 1:5: a court cannot nullify another court's ruling unless it surpasses it in wisdom and number
R. Abbahu: the earlier courts stipulated that anyone later wishing to nullify their decree may do so
Is this ordinance theirs, that they could attach stipulations to it?
It is a halakha transmitted to Moses at Sinai, like the ten saplings, willow branches and water libation
R. Yitzḥak: the prohibition originally applied only thirty days before Rosh HaShana; later Sages extended it, with a stipulation for nullification
Are these prohibitions really halakhot from Sinai, or are they based on explicit verses?
Baraita on Exodus 34:21: plowing and reaping are prohibited in the verse's context
R. Akiva: the Sabbatical prohibition is already stated in Leviticus 25:4, so the Exodus verse must teach plowing before the year
The verse therefore comes to prohibit plowing on the eve of the Sabbatical year

ranges.en: The baraita's scope: plowing that benefits the Sabbatical year and reaping that continues past it
R. Yishmael: the verse refers to Shabbat; only optional reaping is prohibited, unlike the omer mitzva
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak: Sinai halakha permits young saplings until Rosh HaShana, while verses prohibit mature trees
If Sinai tradition permits young saplings, must the prohibition for mature trees also come from Sinai?
The Sinai halakha underlies R. Yishmael's view, while R. Akiva's view rests on verses
R. Yoḥanan: Rabban Gamliel's court annulled the prohibition on the eve of the Sabbatical year based on a Torah source
What is the reason for that view?
Verbal analogy of Shabbat: as Shabbat labor is forbidden only on Shabbat, Sabbatical labor is forbidden only during the year
Rav Ashi objects: a verbal analogy cannot uproot a Sinai halakha or a verse
Rav Ashi: Rabban Gamliel follows R. Yishmael, and the halakha applies only while the Temple stands
Mishna: one may not irrigate a field on Festival intermediate days with cistern rainwater or shaduf water
Shaduf water involves excessive effort, but what excessive effort is there in rainwater?
R. Yoḥanan: a decree equates rainwater with shaduf water; Rav Ashi: rainwater becomes shaduf-like once its level drops
R. Ile'a and Rav Ashi dispute R. Zeira's ruling, which cites Shmuel that streams from pools are permitted
Rav Ashi accepts R. Zeira's ruling, while R. Yoḥanan does not, so rainwater is prohibited regardless
The Gemara restates Shmuel's ruling on streams drawing from pools, for the Festival intermediate days
R. Yirmeya objects from the mishna, which forbids cistern rainwater even if a stream supplies it
R. Zeira replies: the Babylonian pools are like flowing water that never stops, so no concern arises
Baraita: pools filled before the Festival may not be used, but a channel passing between them makes it permitted
Rav Pappa: the allowance applies only when most of the field can be irrigated from that channel
Rav Ashi: it applies even if most of the field cannot be watered at once, since the channel refills over days
Baraita: a pool fed by drips from an irrigated upper field may irrigate a lower field
But the pool may stop flowing and force one to exert himself?
R. Yirmeya: the case is where the upper field still trickles water into the pool
Abaye: the allowance applies only while the first spring that irrigates the upper field has not stopped
Baraita: R. Shimon ben Menasya forbids drawing from the lower bed's channel to irrigate the upper bed
R. Elazar bar Shimon: the same prohibition applies even within a single bed split into lower and higher halves
Baraita: one may draw water for vegetables to eat, but not to improve their growth or appearance
Narrative: Ravina and Rabba Tosefa'a see a man drawing water with a bucket on Festival intermediate days
Rabba Tosefa'a tells Ravina to excommunicate him for transgressing the Sages' words
Ravina cites the baraita: one may draw for vegetables to eat, so he has committed no transgression
Rabba Tosefa'a rejects that reading: madlin means drawing to irrigate vegetables, which is not what it means

ranges.en: Mishna Pe'a 7:5 uses the word meidel for thinning vines, showing it need not mean drawing water
Ravina objects: a baraita permits drawing water to irrigate vegetables for eating
Rabba Tosefa'a concedes: if a baraita states it, the halakha follows it, and he retracts
Mishna: one may not construct circular ditches around grapevines on Festival intermediate days
What are ugiyyot?
Rav Yehuda: they are what are called binkei, circular ditches around vines
A baraita adds that ugiyyot include circular ditches around olive trees and grapevines
Is it really prohibited, given that Rav Yehuda permitted bar Tzitai's family to dig such ditches?
Not difficult: the mishna refers to new ditches, while Rav Yehuda's ruling refers to old ones needing clearing
R. Elazar ben Azarya: one may not construct a new water channel on Festival intermediate days or in the Sabbatical year
Festival prohibition is due to excessive exertion, but why is a channel prohibited in the Sabbatical year?
R. Zeira and R. Abba bar Memel: it appears as hoeing, or it prepares the banks for sowing
What is the practical difference between these two reasons?
If water enters immediately, only the banks-for-sowing reason applies; the hoeing reason is then inapplicable
On the hoeing reason, why not also fear that banks are prepared for planting?
Explained differently: the difference lies in throwing excavated earth far away, which avoids the planting concern
On the banks-for-planting reason, why not also fear it appears as hoeing?
Hoeing is not the concern, since a hoer returns the clod to its place, unlike one who throws the dug earth away
Ameimar taught that R. Elazar ben Azarya prohibits channels because they appear as hoeing, seemingly conflicting with his other view
A mishna (Shevi'it 3:3) on manure heaps, with R. Meir's and R. Elazar ben Azarya's conditions, is raised as a contradiction
R. Elazar ben Azarya's ruling on manure: dig three handbreadths down, raise three up, or place it on a rock
R. Zeira and R. Abba bar Memel resolve it: either the pit was dug in the sixth year, or the pile shows intent to bury manure
Mishna: one may repair a damaged water channel on Festival intermediate days
What is meant by a damaged channel?
R. Abba: a channel that filled with sediment to one handbreadth may be dredged back to its original six handbreadths
The Gemara works out cases: half-to-three and two-to-twelve handbreadths are prohibited, as the work yields little benefit
Is two-to-seven handbreadths permitted, given the extra handbreadth of effort? The dilemma is left unresolved
Abaye permitted the people of Bar Hamdakh to remove river branches on Festival intermediate days
R. Yirmeya permitted the people of Sekhavta to dredge a blocked river
Rav Ashi permitted his townsmen to clean out the nearby Burnitz River
Rav Ashi's reason: the public drinks from it, so it is a public need
The mishna permits tending to all public needs and repairing public channels on Festival intermediate days

ranges.en: Mishnah ruling paraphrased: cleaning out existing cisterns is allowed on Festival intermediate days, but digging new ones is not.
Rabbi Yaakov cites Rabbi Yohanan: the digging ban applies only when the public does not need the cisterns; if they need them, digging is allowed.
The Gemara asks whether digging is really permitted when needed, citing a baraita that seems to forbid digging even for public need.
Reply: that baraita is about a case where the public does not need the cisterns.
Objection: by parallel reasoning, a baraita shows an individual's unneeded cisterns may not even be cleaned, contrary to the proposed reading.
Asks what case the first baraita then describes, if not individual need; the parallel case would forbid digging for public need.
A different baraita permits digging public cisterns when needed, so the first baraita seems contradicted and difficult.
Resolution: the first baraita concerns cleaning an individual's cisterns when needed; public digging is permitted when the public needs it.
Conclusion: digging for the public is forbidden when not needed, and for an individual, even cleaning is forbidden when not needed.
Rav Ashi says the mishna is precise: it lists all public needs, which implies that digging is included.
Asks what the word all adds if not digging, which the mishna would then need to include.
Reply: the word all adds other things taught in a baraita, not digging.
Baraita: court agents go out to clear thorns, repair roads and streets, and fill ritual baths to forty se'a.
Asks from where it is derived that negligent court agents bear guilt for blood shed on the roads.
Teaching: the verse treats anyone responsible for bloodshed on the roads as if they had shed it themselves.
Proof from Deuteronomy 19:10 about innocent blood not shed in the land, and blood upon you.
Objection: the mishna itself explicitly lists road repair and all public needs, so the word all must add digging.
Conclusion: the Gemara infers from this that the mishna permits digging cisterns needed by the public.
Mishna teaching: one may mark graves on Festival intermediate days so passersby avoid impurity.
Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi asks where the Torah alludes to marking graves.
Proof from Ezekiel 39:15: a man sees a bone and sets up a sign beside it.
Ravina asks Rav Ashi: before Ezekiel came, who said graves must be marked?
Rav Ashi replies by citing Rav Hisda, who held that a halakha came from Ezekiel and not from Moses.
Rav Hisda's source: Ezekiel 44:9 on the uncircumcised not entering the Sanctuary.
Ravina repeats the question: before Ezekiel came, who taught that the uncircumcised may not serve?
Reply: such halakhot were learned as a tradition, and Ezekiel later attached a verse to them.
Rabbi Abbahu derives it from Leviticus 13:45, where impurity calls out to the passerby to step away.
Rabbi Uzziel says the same, deriving the call of impurity from the same verse.
Asks why the verse is needed for the statement it is cited for, if it could be stated more simply.
Baraita: the repeated impure teaches that the leper must tell the public of his pain, and the public prays for him.
Reply: a repetition teaches two ideas, that the leper informs others of his plight and that he warns them to stay away.
Abaye derives the grave-marking obligation from Leviticus 19:14, not placing a stumbling block before the blind.
Rav Pappa derives it from Isaiah 57:14, clearing the way of obstacles.
Rav Hinnana derives it from the end of the same Isaiah verse, removing the stumbling block from My people's way.
Rabbi Yehoshua, son of Rav Idi, derives it from Exodus 18:20 about showing the people the way to walk.
Mar Zutra derives it from Leviticus 15:31, warning people to separate from impurity.
Rav Ashi derives it from Leviticus 18:30 about making a safeguard for the charge.
Ravina derives it from Psalms 50:23, marking pure pathways on which it is proper to walk.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: one who weighs his ways and considers how to act properly merits seeing God's salvation.
Exegesis of Psalms 50:23: read the word as vesham, and appraises, rather than vesam, who orders.
Anecdote: Rabbi Yannai's student used to challenge his teachings daily, but did not do so on Festival Shabbat when the public came.

Baraita: courts do not mark an olive-bulk of a corpse or a barleycorn bone, but do mark the spine, skull, or majority of bones.
Baraita: courts mark only uncertain impurity, not known impurity; the uncertain cases are listed as overhangs, protrusions, and beit haperas.
Baraita continues: markers are not placed directly over impurity, nor moved away from it, so as not to waste pure food or Eretz Yisrael.
Restating the baraita's claim that an olive-bulk of a corpse does not impart impurity by means of a tent.
Objection: a baraita explicitly lists an olive-bulk of a corpse among items that impart tent impurity, contradicting the claim.
Rav Pappa: the case is an olive-bulk that will diminish, so it is better to burn offerings temporarily than permanently.
The Gemara explains the baraita's list of uncertain impurities: overhangs, protrusions, and beit haperas.
Overhangs refer to a tree branch hanging over a possible corpse beneath it, forming a tent that imparts impurity.
Protrusions refer to stones jutting from a wall that may cover a corpse, creating a tent over anyone passing under.
Mishna definition: plowing a field with a grave makes it a beit haperas, extending a hundred cubits along the furrow.
Does a beit haperas really impart impurity by means of a tent, given the ruling about blowing across one?
Objection: Shmuel taught that one may blow ahead through a beit haperas while carrying pure items, which implies no tent impurity.
Objection: Ulla's ruling that a trampled beit haperas is pure also implies that a beit haperas does not impart tent impurity.
Rav Pappa distinguishes: the marked case is a field where a grave was lost, while a plowed field is uncertain and imparts no tent impurity.
Is a field where a grave was plowed really called a beit haperas, such that its impurity must be a concern?
Answer: yes, a mishna lists three kinds of beit haperas, including a lost-grave field, a plowed-grave field, and a weepers field.
What is a weepers field?
Rav Yehoshua bar Abba, citing Ulla: a weepers field is where mourners took leave of the deceased before burial.
What is the reason a weepers field carries concern for impurity?
Avimi: because owners may despair of recovering bones, and corpses carried past it may have shed loose limbs there.
Does a field where a grave was plowed not require marking, given the marking rule for such fields?
A baraita: if trees stand in a marked field, a grave was plowed there; if none, a grave was lost, so the ruling conflicts.
Rabbi Yehuda: such signs are relied on only if an elder or scholar can testify, since not everyone is expert in this matter.
Rav Pappa: the baraita concerns a field where a grave was lost and marked immediately; trees indicate later plowing, while no trees indicate loss.
Perhaps the trees were inside the field and the grave outside it, so trees cannot prove the grave was plowed.
As Ulla said, the trees stand on the boundaries next to a public path, so the grave lies between them and was plowed.

ranges.en: Could the impurity lie inside a field while the trees and plowed area sit outside it, so the grave was never plowed?
Reply: trees are scattered over the whole field, so plowing is likely; also the marker sits near the trees, so the grave is near them.
Rabbi Yehuda: signs count only when an elder or scholar can testify, since not everyone knows such matters well.
Abaye infers that a Torah scholar in a town is responsible for the town's affairs and is expected to know what happens there.
Rav Yehuda: one marked stone indicates impurity beneath it; with two stones, lime between them makes the area impure, and no lime makes it pure.
Objection: the area between the stones is ruled pure without any sign of plowing, which a baraita says is impure.
Rav Pappa: the baraita refers to lime poured over the stones, which can fall between them during plowing; without plow marks the area is impure.
Rabbi Asi: marked borders make only those borders impure, while the field's interior stays pure; with all four marked, the whole enclosed field is impure.
Supporting Rabbi Asi, the Gemara cites the baraita that markers are not moved away from impurity so as not to waste Eretz Yisrael.
Mishna: inspectors also go out on Festival intermediate days to uproot diverse kinds that sprouted in the fields.
Do they really go out to uproot diverse kinds during the intermediate days of a Festival?
A contrary mishna says the court issues proclamations about shekels and diverse kinds on the first of Adar, suggesting an earlier time.
The mishna in full: on the fifteenth of Adar they clear roads, measure ritual baths, mark graves, and uproot diverse kinds, raising the question of a second trip.
Rabbi Elazar: the Adar mishna refers to early crops, while the Passover mishna refers to late crops not yet recognizable.
Another view: the Adar mishna refers to tall winter grain, while the Passover mishna refers to later-growing vegetables.
Rabbi Yohanan: they go out in the middle of Adar only when the blossom was not yet recognizable earlier; otherwise they uproot earlier.
Why specifically during the intermediate days of a Festival do they go out to uproot diverse kinds?
Rabbi Yaakov, citing Rabbi Yohanan: workers hired by the court cannot labor on the Festival, so they accept lower wages for public work.
Rav Zevid or Rav Mesharshiyya infers that workers are paid from Temple chamber funds, minimizing costs, rather than by the field owners.
How much of another species mixed into a crop makes it diverse kinds that must be uprooted?
Rav Shmuel bar Yitzhak: the measure is like the mishna's rule about a se'a of seed containing a mixed species.

ranges.en: Rule: if a quarter-kav or more of another species is mixed into the seed, that other species must be reduced by uprooting it.
Objection: a baraita says the Sages ordained that the whole field be declared ownerless, which seems to conflict with uprooting.
Resolution: the uprooting mishna applies before the ordinance, and the ownerless-field baraita applies after it.
Explanation of the earlier practice: court agents uprooted mixed plants and threw them to the owners' livestock, which pleased owners for two reasons.
Explanation of the later ordinances: agents cast the mixed plants on the roads, and finally the whole field was declared ownerless.
Mishna: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov permits drawing water between trees but not watering a whole field, while the Sages permit both cases.
Rav Yehuda: a field that was moist before the Festival may be watered even on the intermediate days.
A baraita confirms this: unwatered plants may not be watered during the Festival, but plants already watered and growing may be.
Restatement: a moist field may be watered, a dry field may not, and the Sages permit both cases.
Ravina infers that sprinkling a garden is permitted on the Festival, because early watering turns a late crop into an early one.
Baraita: one may sprinkle a field of grain during the Sabbatical Year, but not on the intermediate days of a Festival.
Objection: another baraita permits sprinkling a field of grain both on the Festival and during the Sabbatical Year.
Rav Huna: the prohibiting baraita follows Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, and the permitting one follows the Rabbis.
Another baraita: one may sprinkle a white field on the eve of the Sabbatical Year, and sprinkle a grain field during it if the sprouting comes after.
Mishna: one may trap moles and mice in the usual way in orchards and grain fields, and seal wall breaches, on Festival and Sabbatical Year days.
What is meant by the term ishut?
Rav Yehuda: an ishut is an eyeless rodent that digs holes and damages roots; Rava bar Yishmael or Rav Yeimar bar Shelamya gives the identification.
Proof from Psalms 58:9 about a mole that has not seen the sun, which indicates the creature lacks eyes.
Baraita: one may trap moles and mice in fields and orchards in the usual manner, and destroy ant holes so the ants cause no damage.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's method: move soil from one ant hole into another so the ant colonies fight and destroy each other.
Rav Yeimar bar Shelamya, citing Abaye: the method works only when the two nests are separated by a river with no bridge, plank, or rope connection.

ranges.en: How far apart must ant holes be before a river is needed to separate their colonies?
Reply: up to a parasang.
Mishna: Rabbi Yehuda says one may trap rodents in his usual manner in an orchard, but only unusually in a grain field.
Baraita explains the two methods: the usual method is digging a hole and setting a trap; the unusual method is probing and digging out the rodents.
Baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar: the unusual-method limit applies only to grain fields next to a town, not those next to an orchard.
Mishna: one may seal a breach in a garden wall on the intermediate days of a Festival.
How does one seal such a breach?
Rav Yosef: with palm branches and bay branches, which make only a temporary barrier.
Baraita: one fills the breach with stone but does not plaster the stones with clay.
Rav Hisda: this applies to a garden wall, which may wait until after the Festival, but a courtyard wall may be built in the usual manner.
Attempt to support Rav Hisda with a baraita that permits demolishing and rebuilding a leaning wall on the public path, due to danger.
Rejection: that baraita's reason is the danger to passersby, not the protection of the courtyard, so it does not support Rav Hisda.
Some say the baraita refutes Rav Hisda: rebuilding is permitted only for danger, so building a courtyard wall without danger is not allowed.
Rav Hisda's reply: a dangerous leaning wall may be demolished and rebuilt, while an ordinary courtyard wall may be built but not demolished.
If the leaning wall may be demolished, why not allow rebuilding only after the Festival?
Reply: otherwise the owner might refrain from demolishing, leaving the courtyard unprotected, so rebuilding is also permitted.
Rav Ashi: the mishna's wording is precise, since it adds that during the Sabbatical Year one may build in the usual manner, which refers to a garden wall.
If the mishna refers to a courtyard wall, why state it may be built during the Sabbatical Year, since only farm labor is forbidden?
The mention of the garden wall shows the mishna concerns a garden, so Rav Hisda's reading is correct.
Mishna: Rabbi Meir allows a priest to examine a leper on the Festival only to be lenient, while the Rabbis forbid examining in either direction.
Baraita: Rabbi Meir allows examining only to be lenient, Rabbi Yosei forbids both, since examining to be lenient obliges examining to be stringent too.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi: Rabbi Meir fits the quarantined leper case, and Rabbi Yosei fits the confirmed leper case.
Rava: everyone agrees the priest does not examine a pure suspect, or one in the first quarantine week; they disagree only in the other cases.

7b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Meir: whether a suspect is declared pure or impure depends on the priest's discretion; he may stay silent about impurity.
Rabbi Yosei: the verse requires the priest to declare either pure or impure, so he may not remain silent about impurity.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi: Rabbi Yosei is correct for a confirmed leper, and Rabbi Meir for a quarantined one.
Objection: a different baraita says the opposite, that Rabbi Yosei fits the quarantined case and Rabbi Meir the confirmed case.
Reply: this is a dispute among tanna'im following Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi; one holds public company outweighs the leper's isolation.
The other side holds a leper's marital company outweighs public company, so the priest should not examine a confirmed leper on the Festival.
Does this mean a confirmed leper may have relations with his wife?
Yes, that is the implication.
Baraita: the verse about remaining outside the tent for seven days means a counting leper is barred from relations, since tent refers to the wife.
Rabbi Yehuda: the verse in Ezekiel about counting seven days bars relations only during the counting days, not during confirmed leprosy.
Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda: a fortiori, if relations are barred during counting, they are barred even more during confirmed leprosy.
Rabbi Hiyya's anecdote: King Jotham was born during Uzziah's confirmed leprosy, and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi agreed that relations are permitted then.
On what principle do the tanna'im disagree?
Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda: the Torah revealed the ban for counting days, so it applies more strongly to confirmed leprosy; Rabbi Yehuda rejects extra stringencies.
Does this mean the matter depends on the priest's discretion?
Baraita: the phrase on the day it appears implies there are days when the priest examines the symptoms and days when he does not.
Rule: a bridegroom with leprous symptoms gets his seven feast days first, and similarly during a Festival, per Rabbi Yehuda.
Another Sage: no need for the Festival-delay rule, since the verse itself states the priest may delay the house examination.
Leviticus 14:36 on emptying the house before the priest enters: if delay is allowed for optional matters, all the more for a mitzva.
What is the practical difference between these opinions?
Abaye: there is no practical difference, only different interpretations of the verses.
Rava: there is a practical difference, since one view allows delay only for a mitzva and the other also for optional matters.
Why can Rabbi Yehuda not derive delay for optional matters from the house case?
We do not derive a principle from the house case because its halakha is itself a novelty, not a general rule.

8a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: House leprosy is a novelty, since wood and stones are not normally susceptible to impurity, yet a leprous house does become impure.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi: both verses are needed, since one alone would limit delay to a mitzva, and the other extends delay to optional matters and to utensils.
The Master infers from the words on the day it appears that there are days to examine symptoms and days not to examine them.
From where in the verse is this inference drawn?
Abaye: the word but is superfluous unless the examination is conditional, so the verse implies examining only on some days.
Rava: the whole phrase on the day is superfluous unless the examination depends on conditions, so the verse implies examining only on some days.
Abaye's reading: on the day excludes night, so examination is done only by daylight.
From where does Rava derive that examination occurs by day and not at night?
Rava: from the eyes of the priest in Leviticus 13:12, which requires clear sight; Abaye: that verse excludes a priest blind in one eye.
But Rava also needs that verse to exclude a priest blind in one eye.
Yes, that is the case: the verse is the source for the one-eyed priest rule, not the daylight rule.
If so, from where does Rava derive the daylight rule?
Rava: from Leviticus 14:35, the owner says it seems to him a plague as seen by him, not by his light, so the priest also views it by day.
Why does Abaye need his own proof when Rava's verse seems sufficient?
Abaye: Rava's verse could apply only to house leprosy, so on the day is needed to extend daylight-only examination to bodily impurity.
Mishna: Rabbi Meir allows gathering a parent's bones from temporary graves on Festival intermediate days, while Rabbi Yosei forbids it; all forbid lamenting in the thirty days before a Festival.
Baraita: one who gathers a parent's bones mourns all day but not in the evening, which implies that gathering is a cause for mourning, not joy.
Rav Hisda: even bones merely bundled in a sheet cause all-day mourning when buried, supporting the same objection.
Abaye: Rabbi Meir means the joy of the Festival overpowers the pain of gathering the bones, not that gathering itself gives joy.
Mishna: one may not arouse lamentation for a deceased relative during the thirty days before a Festival.
What is meant by not arousing lamentation for a deceased relative?
Rav: a professional eulogizer circulating in the West would call out for mourners, reviving the grief of those recently bereaved.
Mishna: the thirty-day prohibition on lamentation applies before a pilgrimage Festival.
What is different about thirty days that makes this the prohibited period?
Rav Kahana, citing Rav Yehuda and Rav: a man saving money for Jerusalem was delayed when his wife gave his savings to a eulogizer, so the Sages set the thirty-day rule.
Shmuel introduces his own view on the matter, cut off at this point.

8b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The reason: the dead are not forgotten from the heart for thirty days, so grief lingers into the Festival.
What is the practical difference between the two reasons?
The difference appears when the eulogizer works for free, so no money set aside for the Festival is wasted.
Mishna: one may not dig crypts or graves on Festival intermediate days, but may adjust existing crypts, build a laundry pond, and prepare a coffin under conditions.
What are crypts and what are graves?
Rav Yehuda: crypts are dug and graves are built; a baraita says the same.
The mishna teaches that one may adjust previously dug crypts on Festival intermediate days.
How does one adjust a crypt?
Rav Yehuda: shorten a crypt that is too long; a baraita instead says lengthen and widen it to fit the corpse.
The mishna permits constructing a laundry pond on Festival intermediate days.
What is a laundry pond?
Rav Yehuda: a laundry pond is a ditch dug in the ground for washing clothes.
Objection: a baraita lists a laundry pond and a laundry ditch as separate items, implying they differ.
Abaye, or Rav Kahana: the only difference is size, since a laundry pond is larger than a laundry ditch.
The mishna permits preparing a coffin when the mourners share the courtyard with the corpse.
A baraita: one may tend to all the deceased's needs on Festival intermediate days, including cutting boards for a coffin in advance or privately cutting timber.
Mishna: one may not marry on the Festival intermediate days, though one may remarry a divorced wife, since remarriage is less of a joy.
Mishna: a woman may use her usual cosmetics, a layman may sew normally, and bed cords may be woven or tightened, with Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei disagreeing.
If marriage is a source of joy, what is the problem, since rejoicing on a Festival is a mitzva?
Shmuel and others: one may not mix one joy with another, since each joy needs its own celebration.
Rabba bar Rav Huna: the marriage forsakes the rejoicing of the Festival in favor of rejoicing with one's wife.
Abaye tells Rav Yosef that Rabba bar Rav Huna's view is really Rav's, as Rav Daniel bar Ketina reported Rav's teaching.
Rav's proof: Deuteronomy 16:14 says you shall rejoice in your Festival, and not in your wife.
Ulla: the reason is the excessive exertion that wedding preparations require during the Festival.
Rabbi Yitzhak Nappaha: the reason is neglect of procreation, since people would delay marriage to save on separate feasts.
Objection from a baraita: all those whom the Sages forbade to marry on Festival intermediate days, which seems to conflict with the proposed reasons.

9a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Baraita: one may marry on the eve of the pilgrimage Festival.
Objection: this poses a difficulty for all the proposed reasons, since a wedding feast normally spans seven days overlapping the Festival.
If the reason is mixing one joy with another, the difficulty disappears, since the wedding's main joy lasts only one day.
If the reason is excessive exertion, the difficulty disappears, since the main exertion lasts only one day.
If the reason is neglecting procreation, there is no concern, since a man would not delay his wedding to the eve of the Festival.
From where is the principle derived that one may not mix one joy with another?
Proof from Kings 8:65: Solomon did not extend the Temple dedication feast into Sukkot, showing joys are not combined; the Gemara discusses whether it would be permitted if the days coincided.
Perhaps the verse only forbids delaying a wedding to the Festival, and where it coincides a joint feast is allowed.
Reply: Solomon could not leave any part of the Temple building unfinished, so he could not delay the raven-deterring spikes either.
Objection: the raven spikes are a necessary element of the building, so Solomon could not delay them either.
Rather, the verse's redundancy, fourteen days alongside seven and seven, shows the two celebrations must be discrete, just as Festival days must be.
Rabbi Yohanan: Israel did not observe Yom Kippur that year because the dedication feast ran through it, and a Divine Voice assured them of the World-to-Come.
What derivation led them to conclude that the feast overrides Yom Kippur?
A fortiori: if the Tabernacle dedication overrides Shabbat, the permanent Temple dedication with communal offerings overrides Yom Kippur, a lesser punishment of karet.
If they had a sound basis, why were they worried?
The Tabernacle desecrated Shabbat only for sacrificial needs, while the Temple feast involved eating for ordinary needs; no rejoicing is complete without eating and drinking.
From where do we derive that the Tabernacle offerings overrode Shabbat?
Proof from Numbers 7:12 and 7:48 about days; it is not conclusive, since the seventh day may refer to offerings rather than the weekday.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzhak: Numbers 7:72 repeats day for eleven days, showing they were continuous, Shabbat included.
Perhaps the eleven days refer only to days suitable for an individual's offerings, excluding Shabbat.
Another verse, Numbers 7:78, speaks of twelve days as one continuous period, showing the same principle.
Perhaps here too the days are only those suitable for individuals' offerings.
Reply: if so, why are two verses needed to teach the same principle? The repeated phrasing shows the days were consecutive, without a Shabbat break.
From where do we derive that the Temple dedication feast overrides Yom Kippur, so they did not fast?
Verbal analogy: the word day in Kings 8:65 matches the Tabernacle context, so the days were consecutive without a break for Yom Kippur.
A Divine Voice declared that all of them are designated for the World-to-Come.
From where do we derive that God pardoned them for this sin?
Tahlifa's baraita: Kings 8:66 is expounded to show they found their wives pure, enjoyed the Divine Presence, and had sons, and were promised the World-to-Come.
Granted the goodness for Israel was the pardon, but what goodness was done for David His servant?
Rav Yehuda, citing Rav: Solomon's first twenty-four songs failed to open the gates, until his prayer citing David's faithful love opened them, showing David's merit and pardon.
Rabbi Yonatan ben Asmai and Rabbi Yehuda, son of converts, were studying oath laws and took leave of Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai twice, in the evening and morning.
The students cite the rule that a disciple who lodges in the same city must take leave again, from the verses about sending the people away on the eighth and twenty-third days.
Conclusion: from here, a disciple who lodges in the teacher's city must take leave of him once more.
Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai told his son to seek these two men for a blessing; the son found them debating two verses that seemed to conflict.
Apparent contradiction: Proverbs 4:26 says to weigh one's path, while Proverbs 5:6 says do not level the path of life.
Resolution: the first verse concerns a mitzva others can perform, so one weighs what to do personally and what to leave to others.

9b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Resolves that the earlier verse concerns a mitzva that others cannot perform for him.
Two sages pose a contradiction between two verses on whether mitzvot can be compared to Torah.
Distinguishes mitzvot others can perform, which rank below Torah, from ones only he can perform.
Sages bless Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai's son with words that sound like curses.
Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai explains the curses as blessings about children and grandchildren.
Reads the house and lodging imagery as this world versus the World to Come, citing a verse on graves.
Explains the confused table as a large family and the missed new year as a living wife.
Rav blesses Rabbi Shimon ben Halafta, who reports the blessing back as mere words.
The father cites Joel's promise that the people will never be ashamed to show the blessing's weight.
The mishna and a baraita list the cosmetic treatments women may use on intermediate festival days.
Rav Hisda's wife adorns herself before her daughter-in-law; Rav Huna raises a restriction before Rav Hisda.
Rav Huna states that the leniency applies only to a young woman, not an old one.
Rav Hisda objects that even elderly women and a mother may adorn themselves, citing a popular saying.
Rabbi Yehuda says a woman may not apply lime to her skin on the intermediate festival days.
A baraita: Rabbi Yehuda allows lime she can peel off, since later joy outweighs present distress.
Asks whether Rabbi Yehuda truly accepts reasoning that weighs future joy against present distress.
Cites a mishna where Rabbi Yehuda counts only present distress, contradicting that reasoning.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzhak explains that festival halakhot are a special case where later joy matters.
Ravina offers another reading: Rabbi Yehuda always counts the gentile's distress when repaying a debt.
Rav Yehuda describes girls removing hair, what each economic class used, and cites Esther.
Asks what shemen hamor means.
Rav Huna bar Hiyya says it is setaket perfume; Rav Yirmeya says oil from an unripe olive.
A baraita from Rabbi Yehuda: anpikinon is unripe olive oil, which removes hair and softens skin.
Rav Beivai's daughter is depilated limb by limb and fetches a high dowry; a gentile's daughter dies from full application.
Rav Nachman explains Rav Beivai's daughters needed lime because he drank beer, which causes hair growth.

10a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: a layman may sew in his usual manner on the intermediate days of a festival.
Asks what makes someone count as a layman for the sewing rule.
Rabbi Yannai's school and Rabbi Yosei bar Hanina each give a practical test of sewing skill.
Mishna continues: a craftsman may only sew temporary stitches.
Asks what temporary stitching means.
Rabbi Yohanan says skipping stitches; Rabba bar Shmuel says stitches like a dog's teeth.
Mishna: one may interweave the cords of a bed frame on the intermediate days.
Asks what interweaving and tightening the cords actually mean.
Rav Dimi reports that two Sages disagree on these terms, transmitted from earlier authorities.
Lays out the two opposing readings of interweaving and tightening, one for each Sage.
Objects that a baraita says both Meir and Yosei forbid new braiding, which clashes with one reading.
Rav Naḥman challenges Rav Ḥiyya bar Avin with Meir's mishna on three rows of meshes.
Ravin restates the dispute: all agree interweaving means lengthwise and widthwise, so the disagreement lies only in tightening.
Objects with a baraita in which Meir permits interweaving and tightening, while Yosei and others forbid more.
Asks how one could sleep on a bed if even tightening loose cords were forbidden.
Yes, on that view tightening is forbidden, since one can fill the dip with clothing instead.
Mishna: one may set up an oven, stove and mill on intermediate days, but Rabbi Yehuda forbids chiseling new millstones.
Asks what chiseling a millstone means.
Rav Yehuda says cutting grooves into the stone; Rav Yehiel says cutting an eyehole.
Objects with a baraita on setting up ovens and chiseling old and new millstones, with differing views.
If chiseling means cutting an eyehole, why would an old millstone need one, since it already has one?
Replies that the cutting widens an existing hole a little more.
Rav Huna rebukes a man grinding grooves into his millstone and follows the view that forbids it.
Rav Ḥama teaches that grooves may be cut, and trimming hooves or nails is permitted in Rabbi Meir's name.

10b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A donkey turning a mill may not have its hooves trimmed on the intermediate days of a festival.
Rav Yehuda permits trimming a mill donkey's hooves and several mill-related building tasks.
Rava permits grooming a horse and building a trough and bench on the intermediate days.
Rava permits letting an animal's blood for medical purposes during the intermediate days.
Abaye cites a baraita that supports Rava: bloodletting an animal is allowed and its medical care is not withheld.
Rava permits scrubbing garments as part of the laundering process.
Explains that laundering is a layman's work and therefore not prohibited as craftsmanship.
Rav Yitzhak bar Ami, citing Rav Hisda, forbids tying sleeves to create pleats.
Explains that pleating is a craftsman's work, which is prohibited on the intermediate days.
Rava distinguishes clearing ground for a threshing floor, which is permitted, from clearing it for planting, which is forbidden.
Asks what the circumstances of the clearing cases are.
Moving earth between mounds or furrows suggests a threshing floor, but moving it into a furrow suggests planting.
Rava distinguishes clearing twigs for use, which is permitted, from clearing the ground for planting, which is forbidden.
Asks what the circumstances of the twig-clearing cases are.
Taking only the large twigs suggests use; taking large and small ones suggests clearing the ground.
Rava distinguishes opening a water channel to catch fish, which is permitted, from opening it to water the field.
Asks what the circumstances of the water-gate cases are.
Opening two gates suggests fishing; opening one gate suggests watering the field.
Rava distinguishes cutting date palm branches to feed animals, which is permitted, from cutting them to help the palm grow, which is forbidden.
Asks what the circumstances of the palm cases are.
Stripping all branches from one side suggests feeding animals; cutting from both sides suggests tending the palm.
Rava permits cutting unripe dates for eating but forbids preserving them, since they will not be ready until after the festival.
Rav Pappa says the dates are likely to spoil, so they count as goods at risk of loss and may be preserved.
Rava forbids all commerce on the intermediate days of a festival.
Rabbi Yosei bar Avin qualifies this: commerce is permitted where delay would cause a significant loss.
Ravina delays selling a joint business venture until after the festival and profits by doubling its price.
Ravina had lent money to residents of a fortress who would travel away during the year.
Ravina asks Rav Ashi whether he may go to collect the debt during the intermediate days.
Rav Ashi replies that since they are only reachable now, the debt counts as goods at risk of loss and collection is permitted.
A baraita on idolatry is cited as a parallel case: goods at risk of loss may be handled on the festival.

11a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna-style ruling: one may buy property at a gentile fair and have deeds confirmed in their courts, as rescuing a sale.
Rav permits Hiyya bar Ashi to weave simple traps on the intermediate days of the festival.
Explains that simple traps count as a layman's work, so they are allowed.
Complex nets, by contrast, are forbidden on the intermediate days.
Explains that complex nets are a craftsman's work, which is prohibited.
Rav Yehuda permits an oven maker to build ovens and a craftsman to make sieves during the festival.
Objects with a baraita that all agree a new oven may not be built on the intermediate days.
Resolves the conflict: summer ovens dry in time for use, while rainy-season ovens will not be ready.
Mishna: a railing may be built only as a layman's work, and cracks in an oven may be plastered and rolled by hand.
Mishna: hinges, locks and keys may be repaired if not planned in advance, and preserves may be made from edible food.
Asks what makes building a railing a layman's work.
Rav Yosef says a railing of palm and bay branches, not permanently fixed, counts as a layman's work.
Restates the mishna on plastering oven cracks and smoothing them with a roller.
If a roller is allowed, why state that hand or foot is allowed too?
The mishna means the hand or foot may serve as a roller, but not a presser, a craftsman's tool.
Restates the mishna permitting repair of hinges, cylinders, beams, locks and keys on the festival.
Raises a contradiction from a mishna saying workmen's hammers stopped in Jerusalem after the High Priest Yohanan's decree.
Smiths make loud noise and are banned; carpenters are quiet and are allowed.
Rav Hisda objects that this would make only loud noise forbidden and soft noise allowed.
Rav Hisda says sickles make no noise, while chisels do, so the mishnayot concern different tools.
Rav Pappa says one mishna predates Yohanan's decree and the other follows it.
Rav Ashi says the stricter mishna follows Rabbi Yehuda and the permissive one follows Rabbi Yosei.
Ravina applies Rabbi Yosei's view to justify fixing loose nails on the festival.
Mishna: one may preserve food from which one can eat on the festival.
Fish stranded by a flooding river are caught, and Rava permits salting some of them.
Abaye objects that the mishna permits preserving only food one can eat on the festival.
Rava replies that the fish were caught with intent to eat, and leaving them would ruin them, so they are like goods at risk of loss.
Some say that Rava permitted the trapping and salting outright.
Rava permits trapping fish, bringing them home, and salting them.
Abaye objects that heavily salted fish cannot be eaten until they dry out, so preserving them violates the mishna.
Rava says salted fish can be pressed to be edible now, as with Shmuel's fish, and cites his own meals as examples.
Rav is served a fish prepared three ways, with one third cooked, one third salted and one third broiled.
Rav reports that Adda the fisherman said fish that has sat a while and nearly spoiled is at its best.
Rav relays Adda's advice on pairing fish with salt, brine and water, as if they were relatives.
Rav relays Adda's advice to walk after eating fish, cress and milk rather than go straight to bed.
Rav relays Adda's advice to drink water, not beer or wine, after fish and milk, and closes the chapter.

11b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: a mourner whose olives were turned over may load the press and leave it until after the festival, per Rabbi Yehuda.
Rabbi Yosei says he may press and finish the oil in the usual way, since delay would cause loss.
Asks why the mishna opens with mourning but closes with festival rules, leaving the link unclear.
Rav Sheisha son of Rav Idi says it means what is allowed on the festival is forbidden during mourning.
Rav Ashi says the point is that even a Torah-level festival prohibition may be set aside to avoid loss.
A baraita supporting Rav Sheisha lists tasks others may do for a mourner to prevent loss.
Rabbi Yehuda adds that a mourner's plowed or flax field may be sown for him, since sowing time is critical.
The Sages reply that a late-sown field or a different crop can be substituted, so there is no great loss.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds that if no other skilled worker is available, the mourner may do the task himself in private.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds that a public craftsman may work publicly when needed for the festival.
Lists who may have work done for them during mourning, such as tenants and contractors, versus those who may not, such as hired drivers and laborers.
A mourner may not do work hired out to others even if it is by contract.
If contract work is like his own work, why is it prohibited? Non-contract work would look different.
The text should be emended to say the mourner may not do the work whether by contract or not.
If his commission is performed in his own house it may not be done, but in another house it may.
Mar son of Rav Aha detaches his ox from a shared team after a death in his family, to avoid work with his animal.
Rav Ashi objects that a loss to the partner should count, citing the baraita that hired-out animals may work.
Mar holds that an important person must be more stringent, so people do not treat the law lightly.

12a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Shmuel: gentile contractors may not work for a Jew inside the Shabbat limit on his prohibited day, but may outside it.
Rav Pappa limits the outside-limit leniency to places with no nearby city where a Jew could see the work.
Rav Mesharshiyya narrows it further: only Shabbats and festivals, not intermediate days when Jews pass the site.
Mar Zutra's mansion built by gentile contractors outside the limit; Rav Safra and Rav Huna avoid entering it.
Objects that Shmuel's ruling permits such work outside the limit, so Mar Zutra's case seems to conflict.
An important person is held to a stricter standard; alternatively, the contractors were supplied with straw, so they were not independent.
Rav Hama permits the Exilarch's bath attendants to serve him on intermediate days, since they take no pay that week.
Baraita: gentiles may take contracts during the festival for work done after it, but not do the work itself in the week, and never measure or count.
Another baraita: contracts may be taken on the festival with no measuring, weighing or counting, as on a weekday.
Baraita: one may not breed animals on the intermediate days, nor firstborn or unfit consecrated animals, since it resembles labor.
Baraita with Rabbi Yehuda: a she-donkey in heat may be bred to avoid significant loss, while other animals are just brought to males.
Baraita: one may not enclose livestock in a field for manure on festival days, but may allow animals that came on their own.
Baraita: one may not help gentile shepherds fertilize one's field, unless they were hired for a long term.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi allows gentile pasturing as a favor on Shabbat, for food on a festival, and for pay on intermediate days.
Rav Yosef rules that the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi.
Mishna: a wine barrel that may sour may be drawn off during the festival and sealed as usual, per Rabbi Yosei, while Rabbi Yehuda would cover the pit.
Explains why both mishnayot are needed: each one might otherwise be read as limited to oil or wine respectively.
Rav Yitzhak bar Abba asks which tanna requires an altered method even for loss, contradicting Rabbi Yosei.
Rav Yosef rules that the halakha follows Rabbi Yosei, allowing labor to prevent loss in the usual manner.
Students ask Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak whether one may seal a barrel of beer on the intermediate days.
Rav Naḥman cites Rav Yosef, who ruled in accordance with Rabbi Yosei.
The students ask whether Rabbi Yosei's leniency covers beer, which is cheaper, and what the reason for wine is.
The loss is considerable for wine, and beer also loses value if unsealed.
Abaye's foster mother's saying: a sealed six-se'a barrel holds more than an unsealed eight-se'a one.
Rav says the intermediate-day halakhot resemble the halakhot of the Samaritans.
Asks in what aspect of the halakha the two are alike.
Rav Daniel bar Ketina: they are sterile, so one may not derive further rulings from one area to another.
Shmuel permits sealing a jug with pitch but not a barrel; Rav Dimi from Neharde'a holds the reverse.
Each Sage weighs a different concern: Rav Dimi fears financial loss, Shmuel fears exertion.
Abaye states the principle that the intermediate-day halakhot follow the halakhot of Shabbat.

12b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Some actions exempt under Torah law are still prohibited on the festival, while others are permitted ab initio.
Rav Huna had his crop harvested on the intermediate days of the festival.
Rabba bar Rav Huna objects with a baraita allowing grinding only for loss-avoidance, forbidding it otherwise.
Explains the baraita's limits: detached produce may be worked to avoid loss, attached produce may not, and threshing with cattle is excluded.
Rav Huna answers that the baraita is an individual view, and the accepted view is Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's principle in Rabbi Yosei's name.
If the unattributed view is Rabbi Yosei's, threshing with cattle should be allowed too; yet Rav Yitzhak bar Abba says Yosei needs no altered method.
Rabbi Yosei could reply that threshing with cattle is avoided only to prevent public notice, not as an altered method.
Baraita: one may grind, cut wood, and brew beer on festival days for the festival's needs, and leftovers may be used afterward, without contrivance.
Raises a contradiction: a baraita permits brewing with old beer on hand by contriving to prefer new beer.
Resolves it as a tanna dispute: Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda permits the contrivance while others forbid it.
Rav harvested his crop during the intermediate days and Shmuel was dismayed.
Asks whether Shmuel follows Rabbi Yosei's individual view that all labor on attached crops is forbidden.
No, it was wheat that would have been lost if delayed, so Shmuel was only offended by the specific case.
Asks why Rav acted that way.
Rav was in the category of one with nothing to eat, so harvesting was permitted for him.
Asks why Shmuel disapproved if Rav was permitted.
Those who reported to Shmuel omitted details, or an important person like Rav should be stricter.
Rabbi Yehuda Nesia went out on Shabbat wearing a coral seal and drank water heated by a gentile; Rabbi Ami was dismayed.
Rav Yosef asks what the reason for the dismay was, if it was about the coral seal.
A baraita says bracelets, nose rings and rings are ordinary carriable utensils, so the coral seal was allowed.
If Rabbi Ami objected to the heated water, Shmuel said in Rav's name that raw-eaten items heated by gentiles are not prohibited.
An important person is different, and Rabbi Ami expected Rabbi Yehuda Nesia to be stricter.
Rav Ḥananel quotes Rav that one may chop a palm tree on festival days even if only the sawdust is needed; Abaye cursed this.
Rav Ashi had a forest in Shelaniya and went to cut it down during the intermediate days.
Rav Sheila asks Rav Ashi whether he relies on Rav's permission despite Abaye's curse.
Rav Ashi says he did not hear Abaye say that, so he does not follow that view.
Rav Ashi's axe slipped and nearly cut his leg, so he stopped and finished the cutting after the festival.
Rav Yehuda permits uprooting flax and hops and uprooting sesame on the intermediate days of the festival.
Abaye asks what use sesame has, since its seeds need a long drying period before oil can be extracted.
Rav Yosef replies that sesame is useful for its seeds, which can be eaten at once.
Rabbi Yannai harvested his orchard during the festival to avoid spoilage, and then declared that year's earnings ownerless to prevent a bad example.
Mishna: one may bring in fruit or draw out flax on festival days to prevent loss, if the labor was not planned in advance.
Baraita: produce may be brought in because of thieves, but discreetly, into the house.
Rav Yosef brought beams into his house during the day on a festival.
Abaye objects that the baraita requires bringing items in discreetly.
Rav Yosef says daytime moving is the discreet method, since at night more people and torchbearers would draw attention.
Mishna: flax may be drawn out of the soaking pool, but labor planned in advance is destroyed.
Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Zeira whether a man who planned labor for the festival and then died should have his children penalized.
