ranges.en: Case of one who blemished a firstborn animal: the Sages penalized his son after him, since the prohibition is biblical.
Proposes the same penalty explanation for selling a slave to a gentile: each day in gentile hands bars mitzvot.
Asks whether the penalty falls on the man himself or on his money, when he worked on the intermediate days.
Rabbi Zeira cites a Shevi'it mishna and Rabbi Yosei bar Ḥanina's tradition: the penalty falls on the offender, not his son.
Abaye's tradition: no penalty on the son for non-evident damage to another's pure items; only the offender is penalized.
Mishna: houses, slaves and cattle may be bought on the intermediate days only for the festival or for a seller with nothing to eat.
Rava asks Rav Naḥman whether a poor worker may be given work on the intermediate days.
Rav Naḥman cites the mishna's needy-seller clause; Rava replies it merely explains what the seller's needs are.
Abaye objects with a mishna permitting notes for a needy lender, implying wages for needy workers are allowed.
Rav Sheshet objects with a Pesaḥim mishna allowing three crafts to work on the eve of Passover, with tailors allowed as on the festival.
If paying a needy worker is permitted, then all such labor should be permitted on the eve of Passover too.
Rav Pappa objects that by the same logic building a leaning wall should be permitted on the eve of Passover.
Ravina objects that by the same logic a scribe writing documents should be permitted on the eve of Passover.
Rav Ashi replies the two cases differ: festival labor is for exertion, while eve-of-Passover prohibitions serve the festival's needs.
Mishna: one may move possessions only within a courtyard if needed, and may fetch utensils from a craftsman only if they risk theft.
Asks how the mishna can forbid moving possessions at all, then permit moving them between courtyards.
Abaye explains the latter clause means moving items within the same courtyard.
Mishna: one may not bring utensils home from a craftsman's house.
Rav Pappa reports Rava's test: a mishna permitting carrying utensils to and from a craftsman, even without festival need, seems to conflict.
Raises the contradiction: one mishna permits moving craftsmen's utensils even when not needed for the festival.
Reconciles it two ways: one applies to the eve of Passover, or the craftsman is trusted in one case and not the other.

13b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Baraita: utensils may be fetched from a craftsman's house, and if he is unreliable, moved to a safe place or brought home discreetly.
Resolves the apparent contradiction: one mishna refers to the eve of Passover, the other to the intermediate days.
Mishna: figs may be covered with straw, condensed per Rabbi Yehuda, and sellers and tradesmen may work in private, per Rabbi Yosei's stringency.
Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba and Rabbi Asi disagree in Ḥizkiyya's and Rabbi Yoḥanan's name on what covering and condensing mean.
A baraita supports the reading that condensing means piling the figs like a heap of grain, as Rabbi Yehuda said.
Restates the mishna: sellers of produce, clothing and utensils sell in private for the festival, and Rabbi Yosei calls it a stringency.
Asks whether the stringency means they never worked at all, or only worked in private.
Cites a baraita: Rabbi Yosei's stringencies for Tiberias, Akko and Tzippori are to refrain from the work entirely.
Abaye explains hilka, targis and tisanei as grains broken into two, three and four; Rav Dimi says hilka is emmer.
Objects that hilka, targis and tisanei are impure everywhere, which fits Abaye's reading but not Rav Dimi's.
Explains the baraita applies to husked emmer, and hilka is named for the removed husks.
Objects with a vow baraita: rice and groats are permitted to a vower of grain, which fits Abaye's reading but not Rav Dimi's.
Rav Huna permits spice merchants to sell in the usual way in the marketplace on the intermediate days.
Rav Kahana objects with a baraita: a shop opening onto the public street may open only one door, except before the last festival day.
Distinguishes: the baraita concerns fruit, bought in bulk, while Rav Huna's ruling concerns spices, bought in small amounts.
Closes the chapter, which opens with the words he who turned over.
Mishna: travelers from overseas, released prisoners, and certain ritually cleansed or released people may shave on the intermediate days.
Mishna: the same people may also launder their clothes on the intermediate days.

14a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: those released from ostracism or vows, and ritually impure people returning to purity, may launder on the festival; others may not.
Asks why everyone else is barred from these actions rather than allowed under the festival's honor.
Cites a Taanit mishna: priestly watch members may not cut hair or launder during their week until Thursday.
Rabba bar bar Ḥana, citing Rabbi Elazar, says the rule keeps people from entering their week or the festival unkempt.
Rabbi Zeira asks whether a man who lost an item before the festival may cut hair and launder on the intermediate days.
Abaye says the Sages do not grant exceptions whose reason is not clearly evident, citing the Syrian cakes of Baitos.
Rabbi Zeira retorts that Rabbi Yoḥanan's leniency for a man with one shirt would likewise need an evident reason.
Mar son of Rav Ashi answers that the belt shows the man has only one shirt, so the reason is evident.
Rav Ashi's version: is a craftsman who lost an item before the festival permitted to cut and launder? Unresolved.
Mishna: one who comes from overseas may cut his hair, but the Gemara notes this is not Rabbi Yehuda's view, per a baraita.
Rava distinguishes leaving to travel, which is forbidden, from leaving for basic needs, which is allowed, and leaving for profit, which is disputed.
A baraita attributed to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi seems internally inconsistent when read through Rava's distinctions.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi did not decide between the views; he clarified that they agree in the clear cases and dispute only the profit case.
Shmuel: a baby born on the festival may have long hair cut on the intermediate days, but one born earlier may not.
Rav Pineḥas objects with a baraita that cutting hair on the festival days is linked to cutting it during mourning.

14b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: If a minor is subject to a distinction, he would bear mourning, but a baraita says minors do not observe mourning; Rav Ashi calls the inference weak.
Shmuel rules a child's hair may be cut on the festival, whether he was born before or during it.
Rav Pineḥas cites a baraita: those permitted to shave on the festival may also shave during mourning, supporting Shmuel.
If a child may not be shaved, mourning would apply to a minor, which the baraita about rending garments contradicts.
Rav Ashi again objects that the inference is only a possibility, so it does not clearly support Shmuel.
A mourner does not observe mourning practices on a festival, based on the verse about rejoicing in the festival.
An earlier mourning overrides the festival rejoicing, but a death during the festival does not override the community's obligation.
Asks whether an ostracized person keeps his ostracism during the festival, or whether the festival overrides it.
A fortiori: if the festival suspends ostracism, courts could not ostracize someone during the festival, so ostracism must apply.
Abaye and Rav Yosef object that courts would have to execute on the festival, and that the rejoicing of judges would be prevented.
Judges deliberate in the morning, eat and rejoice, and return near sunset to issue the verdict.
A baraita: the Sages permitted an ostracized person to cut his hair on the intermediate days, implying the status otherwise applies.
Rava objects that the baraita says they permitted him, which means only an individual who appeased his litigant was released.
Asks whether a leper keeps the rules of his leprosy during the festival, or whether the festival overrides them.
Abaye cites a baraita on the nazirite and the leper who regain purity: the baraita implies the leper observes his status during impurity.
The baraita's wording is a needless-to-say formula: during impurity the leper does not observe the rules, but regaining purity is allowed to shave.
Rava cites the High Priest, whom the verse about the leper includes; he observes his status during the year, like any mourner.
A mourner's haircut is forbidden, derived from the verse to the sons of Aaron not to let their hair go loose.

15a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks what the halakha is for ostracized people and lepers regarding haircuts.
A baraita says ostracized people and lepers may not cut hair or launder clothes.
A baraita: when an ostracized person dies still under ban, the court places a large stone on his coffin.
A mourner must wrap his head, derived from God's instruction to Ezekiel not to cover his lip, implying others must.
Asks whether an ostracized person must wrap his head like a mourner.
Rav Yosef cites a baraita on fast-day participants: they wrap themselves like the ostracized and mourners.
Abaye objects that Heaven's ban is more severe, so it may differ from an earthly ban.
Asks whether a leper must wrap his head.
A verse says a leper covers his upper lip, which by inference shows he wraps his head.
A mourner may not wear phylacteries, derived from Ezekiel's special command to bind headwear.
Asks whether an ostracized person may wear phylacteries; the question is left unresolved.
Asks whether a leper may wear phylacteries.
A baraita on the leper's garments and head, with Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva's readings, suggests the leper may not wear phylacteries.
Rav Pappa says the verse may mean a cap or scarf, not phylacteries; the rule is excess adornment.
A mourner may not greet or be greeted, derived from Ezekiel's command to sigh in silence.
Asks whether an ostracized person may greet others.
Rav Yosef cites the fast-day baraita: those reprimanded by Heaven may not greet one another.
Abaye objects that Heaven's ban is more severe, so the proof does not settle the earthly case.
Asks whether a leper may greet others.
A leper's covered lip implies he is like the ostracized and mourner, and so may not greet.
Rav Aḥa bar Pineḥas says the baraita only treats the leper like those two in other respects, so no proof about the ostracized arises.
A mourner may not study Torah, derived from Ezekiel's command to be silent.
Asks whether an ostracized person may study Torah.
Rav Yosef cites a baraita: the ostracized may study alone and may run a small shop, but not teach or be taught.
Rav says the small shop was selling water in a dry valley, a modest livelihood.
Asks whether a leper may speak words of Torah.
A baraita from Deuteronomy: Torah must be studied with reverence, as at Sinai, so the leper may study.
Zavim, lepers and those who have intercourse with menstruants may read and study Torah, but those with seminal emission may not.
A mourner may not launder clothes, derived from the account of Joab's wise woman feigning mourning.
Asks whether ostracized people and lepers may launder clothes.
A baraita says the ostracized and lepers may not cut hair or launder clothes, so they may not launder.
A mourner must rend his clothes, derived from the command to Aaron's sons not to rend theirs.
Asks whether an ostracized person must rend his clothes; unresolved.
A baraita: the leper's garments must be torn, so the leper must rend clothes.
A mourner must overturn his bed to sleep on its underside, as bar Kappara's baraita states.

15b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: God says humans were made in His image, which is overturned by death, so mourners overturn their beds.
Asks whether an ostracized person or a leper must overturn the bed; the question is left unresolved.
A mourner may not work, derived from Amos's verse turning festivals into mourning, so mourning days match festival rules.
Asks whether an ostracized person may perform work.
Rav Yosef cites a baraita: work is forbidden during the day of a fast but allowed at night, and the rest of the rules are not about work.
Another baraita allows an ostracized person to be hired and to hire others, so he may work.
Asks whether a leper may perform work; unresolved.
A mourner may not bathe, derived from the verse not to anoint oneself, since bathing counts as anointing.
Asks whether an ostracized person may bathe.
Rav Yosef cites a baraita: on a communal fast one may wash face, hands and feet, and the rest of the rules are not about bathing.
The Gemara rejects the inference: the rule about the rest of the prohibitions does not extend to bathing.
Asks whether a leper may bathe; unresolved.
A mourner may not wear shoes, derived from God's instruction to Ezekiel to put his shoes on his feet.
Asks whether an ostracized person may wear shoes.
Rav Yosef cites a baraita: on a fast one may wear shoes on the road but not in the city, and the rest of the rules are not about shoes.
The Gemara rejects the inference: the rule about the rest of the prohibitions does not extend to wearing shoes.
Asks whether a leper may wear shoes; unresolved.
A mourner may not have marital relations, inferred from David's comforting of Bath-Sheba only after the death.
Asks whether an ostracized person may have marital relations.
Rav Yosef cites that the Israelites in the wilderness were ostracized yet had children, so the ostracized may have relations.
Abaye objects that Heaven's ban may be less severe than an earthly ban, so the wilderness proof fails; the Gemara notes Abaye's own inconsistency.
Asks whether a leper may have marital relations.
A baraita on the leper staying outside his tent: the tent means the wife, so the leper is barred from relations.
Asks whether the leper ruling settles the ostracized person's case.
Rav Huna son of Rav Pineḥas says the baraita only treats the leper like the ostracized in other respects, adding the marital ban, so nothing follows for the ostracized.
A mourner may not send offerings, per Rabbi Shimon's baraita: shelamim are only sacrificed when one is whole and settled.
Asks whether an ostracized person may send his offerings.
Rav Yosef cites that the wilderness Israelites were ostracized yet sent offerings, so the ostracized may send them.
Abaye objects that Heaven's ban may be less severe than an earthly ban, so the proof fails.
The Gemara explains Abaye is uncertain which ban is more severe, so he rejects Rav Yosef's arguments in both directions.
Asks whether a leper may send his offerings.
A baraita on Ezekiel's priest after impurity: the seven-day count precedes his sacrifice, which proves the leper may send offerings only after purification.
