ranges.en: Rabbi Yehuda rules the priest's meal-offering of a tenth of an ephah is not brought while he is impure.
Rabbi Shimon derives from Ezekiel's verse that a leper, unfit to enter the Temple, cannot send offerings.
Rava derives from Numbers how a court sends an agent to summon a defendant before any ostracism.
Verses on Korah show the summons names the great man, both parties, a set date, and a postponed second date.
Dathan and Abiram's insult to the court's agent is reported back to Moses and does not count as slander.
Verses on Meroz show ostracism for disobeying a summons, a curse on those who sit near, and public detailing of the sin.
Ulla says Barak ostracized Meroz with four hundred shofarot; some say Meroz was a man, others a star.
Ezra's verse shows a court may declare the property of one who ignores its summons ownerless and separate him.
Nehemiah's verse shows the court may contend with, curse, beat, and make such a person swear.
Ezra's verse shows the court may shackle, chain, and press one who refuses the judgment.
Asks what lishroshi means in Ezra's verse.
Adda Mari says it means pressure, traced through Rav Yehuda to Nehemya bar Baruch's teaching.
Asks what pressure means.
Rav Yehuda son of Rav Shmuel says the procedure is ostracism at once, again after thirty days, and excommunication after sixty.
Rav Ḥisda's rule, relayed by Rav Huna bar Ḥinnana: warn three times over monetary debts, but ostracize at once for disrespect to a scholar.
A butcher insulted Rav Tuvi bar Mattana; Abaye and Rava ostracized him, and he later appeased Rav Tuvi.
Abaye asks whether the butcher should be released before thirty days, given the Sages cannot buy his meat.
Rav Idi bar Avin cites Shmuel that a shofar blast imposes and releases; Abaye limits this to monetary cases.
Apparently Abaye holds that three people cannot be released by three others, since he did not delegate the release.
Asks whether three others may release one whom three people ostracized.
A baraita on teacher, student, city and Nasi ostracism, showing each participant voids his own portion and three others may not void it.
Ameimar rules that three others may come and release one whom three ostracized.
Rav Ashi objects with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's baraita, saying a dead student's portion cannot be voided at all.
Baraita: ostracism lasts at least thirty days and admonition at least seven, alluded to in Miriam's seven days.
Rav Ḥisda: our ostracism in Babylonia carries the force of admonition in Eretz Yisrael, which lasts seven days.
Objects that Eretz Yisrael's admonition seems to last longer, citing a dispute between Rabbi Shimon and bar Kappara.
Rabbi Shimon says the matter needs his father, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, to resolve; bar Kappara mocks him.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi rebukes bar Kappara, who takes it to heart and accepts a thirty-day self-admonition.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi decrees that students be taught in a study hall, not the marketplace, based on the Song of Songs verse.

16b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Words of Torah, like God's work, should stay hidden in the study hall.
Rabbi Ḥiyya defies the nasi's decree, teaching in the marketplace; the nasi rebukes him and he accepts a thirty-day self-admonition.
On the thirtieth day the nasi sends for Rabbi Ḥiyya, then sends a second message telling him not to come.
Asks what the nasi held at first and what he held in the end about part of a day counting as a whole day.
Rabbi Ḥiyya comes on the same day, says he obeyed the first message, and the nasi sees divine favor in him.
Asks why Rabbi Ḥiyya taught in the marketplace against the nasi's instruction.
Rabbi Ḥiyya cites Proverbs: wisdom cries aloud in the streets.
The nasi rebuts: a verse read three times must be understood properly, so the verse does not support his action.
The verse is read in light of Rava: one who studies Torah privately has his knowledge proclaimed outside.
Asks how Isaiah's verse, I have not spoken in secret, fits this.
That verse refers to the kalla gatherings in Elul and Adar, when public teaching is allowed.
Rabbi Ḥiyya reads the thighs verse as about charity, so the thirty-day admonition is not conclusive for Eretz Yisrael.
Asks how long the admonition lasts in Babylonia.
Admonition in Babylonia is one day: Mar Ukva showed Shmuel respect, and when Shmuel felt slighted, Mar Ukva accepted one day's admonition.
Mar Ukva failed to notice Shmuel following him home; Shmuel's complaint led Mar Ukva to accept a day's admonition.
A woman refused to move her leg for a scholar; Rav Naḥman ruled a single day of admonition since no formal ban was pronounced.
Zutra bar Toviyya reads David's last words and asks Rav Yehuda about the first words.
Zutra asks what David's first words were, if last words imply first ones.
Rav Yehuda ignores the question; Zutra repeats it and is rebuked, and accepts a day's self-admonition.
Asks what David's first words were, if the verse mentions last words.
The first words are the song in 2 Samuel 22:1, which the Gemara treats as words.
God rebukes David for singing over Saul's fall, since Saul was dearer in his own right.
David's psalm concerning Cush the Benjaminite: Cush is read as Saul's nickname for his dark and unusual conduct.
Parallel verses about Zipporah, Ebed-Melech and Zedekiah are read the same way: Cush denotes character, not skin.
Amos's verse about Israel as Cushites is read as Israel being distinct for its actions among the nations.
Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani and Rabbi Yonatan read the verse in David's last words as a tradition of repentance.
The verse about the God of Israel and a righteous ruler is quoted for interpretation.
Asks what the verse is saying.
Rabbi Abbahu says the righteous man nullifies God's decree, so the verse describes the righteous person's power.
The verse listing David's warriors is quoted as a list of names.
Asks what the verse is saying.
Rabbi Abbahu says these are not names but descriptions of David's deeds, including his humility of sitting on the ground.
David taught the Sages seated on the ground after his teacher Ira died, and refused their offer of cushions.
Rav says God rewarded David's humility: he may nullify divine decrees, becoming like God.
David was head of the three Patriarchs, softened as a worm in study and hardened as a tree in battle, sighing over the missing two hundred.
A divine voice explains the unfulfilled promise: David's sin with Uriah prevented full fulfillment.
Tradition chain for a statement on ostracism, attributed to Rabbi Tanḥum, Rav Huna, and others.

17a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A baraita: ostracism by a student over his own dignity is valid against all but his teacher, so the teacher is not bound.
Clarifies that a ban for sin would bind the teacher too, so the case must be a personal insult; the verse on wisdom supports this.
Rav Yosef holds a scholar may act on his own certain knowledge and ostracize one who insults him, without a court.
A scholar of ill repute is discussed, whom the Sages need but whose conduct desecrates God's name.
Rav Yehuda asks what should be done about this scholar, since excommunication and leaving him alone are both problematic.
Rabbi Yoḥanan's reading of Malachi: seek Torah from a teacher who is like an angel of the Lord, and not from one who is impure.
Rav Yehuda ostracizes the scholar; when Rav Yehuda falls ill the scholar visits, and Rav Yehuda laughs at him.
Rav Yehuda explains he laughed out of happiness: he never flattered the scholar and judged him fairly by halakha.
After Rav Yehuda's death, the scholar seeks release; the Sages send him to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who sends Rabbi Ami to examine it.
Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani objects: even the Nasi's maidservant's ostracism was not lightly revoked, so this ban should not be revoked either.
Rabbi Zeira reads the timing of Rabbi Shmuel's arrival as a sign from Heaven, so Rabbi Ami does not release the scholar.
A wasp stings the ostracized scholar, who dies; he is buried in the judges' caves after the pious caves reject him.
Asks why the scholar was accepted in the judges' caves.
He had acted on Rabbi Ilai's teaching: one who cannot resist his inclination should mourn in black and sin privately, not publicly.
Asks what the story of the Nasi's maidservant involves.
The maidservant rebukes a man for hitting his adult son, citing the stumbling-block prohibition for the blind.
Reish Lakish ostracizes a man who ate figs from his orchard; the man replies that Reish Lakish's own ban is no ban.
The Sages tell Reish Lakish the man's ban is valid but his own is not, since it was a personal matter.
Reish Lakish asks what remedy exists for a ban he cannot lift because he does not know the man.
The Sages send him to the Nasi, who can release a ban whose issuer is unknown.
Rav Huna says in Usha a court president who sins is not publicly ostracized, but told to stay home to protect God's name.
Reish Lakish disagrees: a Torah scholar is not ostracized publicly, citing Hosea's night-and-day imagery.
Mar Zutra first ostracizes himself as a mark of honor to the scholar, then ostracizes the scholar, then releases both on lodging.
Rav Giddel quotes Rav that a scholar may ostracize himself; Rav Pappa notes that in the West lashes are used instead of ostracism.
Asks what the word shamta means.
Rav says it means there is death, and Shmuel says desolation, like fat on an oven that lingers after the ban is lifted.
Reish Lakish's view is that the ban enters and leaves all 248 organs, which disagrees with Rav and Shmuel's readings.
The numerical value of herem (248) and raḥem (248) shows the ban enters all organs and leaves them all when revoked.
Rav Yosef says a ban placed on a dog's tail took effect, as a dog that ate the Sages' shoes was burned.
Rav Yosef tells a scholar troubled by a violent man to publish a written ban and place it in a jug.

17b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A man buried a jug in a cemetery and sounded shofarot for forty days; the jug broke and he died.
Why are shofarot sounded at excommunication, and why is a broken blast sounded?
Rav Yitzhak bar Yehuda explains that the broken blast breaks even tall buildings, meaning the powerful.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's baraita: when the Sages set their eyes on someone, it brings death or poverty.
The mishna teaches that a nazirite and a leper may cut their hair on the intermediate days of a festival.
Rabbi Yirmeya asks whether this allowance applies only when there was no time to cut hair before the festival.
Rabbi Zeira answers from a baraita: the allowance requires no free time, but nazirites and lepers are allowed even with time.
A baraita teaches that a priest and a mourner may cut their hair on the intermediate days of a festival.
What are the circumstances of the mourner's case?
If his eighth day fell on the eve of the festival, he should have cut his hair before the festival, so that cannot be it.
Rather, his eighth day fell on Shabbat, which was the eve of the festival.
But then he should have cut his hair on Friday, the eve of Shabbat.
Rav Hisda cites Ravina bar Sheila: the halakha follows Abba Shaul, and the Rabbis concede that one may cut on Friday.
No, the baraita refers to a case where the seventh day of mourning falls on Shabbat, the eve of the festival.
The baraita follows Abba Shaul, who counts part of a day as a whole; our mishna follows the Rabbis, who do not.
What are the circumstances of the priest's case?
If his watch was completed on the eve of the festival, he should have cut his hair before the festival.
No, the baraita refers to a priest who completed his watch during the festival week itself.
The tanna of our mishna holds that a watch is considered incomplete when it is only completed during the festival.
The mishna teaches that in the three festivals all watches share equally in festival offerings and in the shewbread.
So the priest is like one whose watch was not completed during the festival, and he may not cut his hair until after it.
The baraita's tanna holds that although he shares other watches, his own watch was completed, so he may cut his hair.
The Sages taught that those allowed to cut hair on festival days may also cut hair during their mourning if prevented earlier.
But isn't it taught that they are prohibited from cutting hair during their mourning?
Rav Hisda, citing Rav Sheila, answers that the permissive baraita refers to two mourning periods following one another.
If it refers to succession, why does it say all those, when the allowance should apply to everyone?
A baraita: if mourning periods follow one another and hair grows heavy, he may cut with a razor and wash clothes in water.
Rav Hisda explains: cutting means with a razor and washing means with water, and a mourner may generally not launder.
The Sages taught that cutting nails on festival days is prohibited like cutting hair; Rabbi Yehuda holds this, Rabbi Yosei permits it.
Likewise a mourner may not cut nails during mourning; Rabbi Yehuda holds this, Rabbi Yosei permits it.
Ulla rules that the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda for mourning and Rabbi Yosei for festival days; Shmuel's view begins the next sentence.

18a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The halakha follows Rabbi Yosei for festival and mourning, as Shmuel said: follow the more lenient view in mourning.
Pinehas, Shmuel's brother, suffered a bereavement, and Shmuel came to console him and noticed his long nails.
Shmuel asked Pinehas why he had not cut his nails.
Pinehas replied: if it were your relative and you were mourning, would you be so careless about your appearance?
Pinehas's words came true, as Ecclesiastes says that an error proceeds from a ruler.
Shmuel then cut his own nails and threw them at Pinehas's face, telling him a covenant is made with the lips, as Rabbi Yohanan taught.
Rabbi Yohanan derives that speech shapes outcomes from Abraham's words in Genesis 22:5 that they would return.
The two men concluded that a mourner may cut his hand nails but not his foot nails, and this was the initial reading.
Rav Anan bar Tahlifa explained that Shmuel himself taught that hand and foot nails are treated alike.
Rav Ḥiyya bar Ashi cites Rav that cutting nails with scissors made for nails is prohibited.
Rav Shemen bar Abba saw Rabbi Yohanan bite his nails with his teeth on the festival intermediate days.
The Gemara draws three lessons from this: nails may be cut on festival days, are not repulsive, and may be thrown away.
Is that so? A baraita says burying nails is righteous, burning them pious, and throwing them away wicked.
What is the reason that throwing away nail clippings is prohibited?
Lest a pregnant woman walk over them and miscarry.
A woman is not usually in the study hall, and nails swept outside change their status, so they are no longer harmful.
Rav Yehuda cites Rav: two Sages from Hamatan asked Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi about cutting nails, and he permitted it.
He would also have permitted trimming the mustache if they had asked about it.
Shmuel reports that they did ask about the mustache, and he permitted it.
Avitul cites Rav Pappa: the mustache may be trimmed from one corner of the mouth to the other.
Rabbi Ami permits trimming only the part that interferes with eating; Rav Naḥman bar Yitzhak says his whole mustache interferes.
Avitul cites Rav Pappa: Pharaoh in Moses's day was a cubit tall, with a cubit-long beard and a short body.
The description of Pharaoh's lowliness is supported by Daniel 4:14 about setting over him the lowest of men.
Avitul also cites Rav Pappa: Pharaoh was a sorcerer who regularly went out to the water.
Exodus 7:15 says Pharaoh goes out to the water, supporting the claim he practiced sorcery.
The mishna teaches that people coming from overseas may launder their clothes on the intermediate days of a festival.
Rav Asi cites Rabbi Yohanan: anyone with only one shirt may launder it on the intermediate days of a festival.
Rabbi Yirmeya objects from the mishna: those listed may launder, which implies someone with only one shirt may not.
Rabbi Ya'akov explains that the mishna refers to people who have two dirty garments, while Rabbi Yohanan refers to one garment.
Rav Yitzhak bar Ya'akov sends word from Rabbi Yohanan that linen garments may be laundered on the festival intermediate days.
Rava objects from the mishna about hand towels, which are not clearly covered by that ruling.

18b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rava's objection continues: the mishna's list of towels implies other linen garments may not be laundered on festival days.
Abaye replies that there is no contradiction, since the mishna refers to other materials and linen may be laundered.
Bar Hedya reports seeing basins of linen garments laundered at the Sea of Tiberias on festival intermediate days.
Abaye objects that this report proves nothing, since they may have acted without the Sages' consent.
The mishna lists documents that may be written on festival intermediate days, such as betrothal and divorce documents and court records.
Shmuel rules that one may betroth a woman on festival intermediate days, lest another betroth her first.
The Gemara suggests the mishna's list, which includes betrothal documents, supports Shmuel.
Does the mishna mean actual betrothal, or only documents recording the parents' stipulations?
Rav Giddel cites Rav: the mishna means stipulation documents, since such agreements are binding through words alone.
A mishna says one may not marry, nor perform levirate marriage, on festival days because it is a joyous occasion.
That mishna is stated as a needless-to-say case: betrothal is obviously excluded, and marriage is excluded too.
A baraita from Shmuel's school permits betrothal but forbids marriage and levirate on festival days.
Did Shmuel really fear that another man would betroth her first, given the Divine Voice that predestines matches?
Rav Yehuda cites Shmuel that a Divine Voice predestines each match, which seems to make the fear unnecessary.
Rather, Shmuel feared that a rival might pray for mercy and change the predestined match.
Rava's anecdote about a man praying for a specific wife illustrates that prayer can alter a predestined match.
Rav cites Rabbi Reuven ben Itzterobili: a match between a man and woman is decreed from God, and he begins to support this from the Torah.
Verses from the Torah, Prophets and Writings, such as Genesis 24:50 and Proverbs 19:14, support that matches are from God.
Rabbi Reuven ben Itzterobili teaches that a person is suspected only when he has actually done something wrong or at least intended it.
Rabbi Ya'akov objects from II Kings 17:9 that people invent baseless accusations against others.
There they invented accusations to anger God, but they did not truly believe them.
Psalms 106:16 is cited as a challenge, showing that men suspected Moses of wrongdoing without basis.
Rav Shmuel bar Yitzhak explains that every man warned his wife against Moses out of jealousy, suspecting falsely.
There they acted out of hatred for Moses and did not truly suspect him.
Rabbi Yosei's wish to share the future world with the falsely suspected is cited as a challenge to the rule.
Rav Pappa says he himself was suspected of a wrongdoing but was innocent.
The cases differ: one is a rumor that stops, which may be baseless, while the other is a rumor that does not stop.
For how long must a rumor persist to count as one that does not stop?
Abaye says his nurse taught him that local gossip lasts a day and a half, after which it is a persistent rumor.
Abaye's rule is refined: a stopped rumor is baseless only if it stopped on its own and did not recur, and only without enemies.
The mishna forbids writing debt bills on festival days, except if the lender distrusts the borrower or the scribe needs food.
The mishna forbids writing Torah scrolls, phylacteries and mezuzot on festival days, though Rabbi Yehuda permits writing them for oneself.

19a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The mishna permits spinning sky-blue wool for fringes on the thigh, but not with an ordinary spindle on festival days.
A baraita gives three views on writing and selling phylacteries and fringes for oneself: Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei.
Rav ruled for Rav Ḥananel, and the halakha follows Rabbi Yosei: write and sell in the usual manner, enough for a livelihood.
The mishna and a baraita dispute spinning fringe wool with a stone or a spindle, with Rabbi Eliezer forbidding the stone.
Shmuel and Rabbi Yoḥanan rule that spinning with a stone or spindle is permitted, and writing and selling follow the usual manner.
The mishna says burial before a festival cancels the seven- or thirty-day mourning decree, and the Sages explain that Shabbat does not interrupt mourning but festivals do.
Rabbi Eliezer and Rabban Gamliel differ on Shavuot, Rosh HaShana and Yom Kippur; the Rabbis rule each is treated as Shabbat or as a festival.
Rav, Rav Huna and Rav Sheshet debate whether the mourning days themselves were cancelled or only the prohibitions.
What is the reason that the mourning days were not entirely cancelled?
So that a mourner who cut hair before the festival but not on its eve must keep the thirty-day restrictions afterward.

19b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: But a baraita says burial three or eight days before a festival cancels the mourning decrees, so haircutting on the eve is needed.
Abba Shaul says a mourner who did not cut hair on the eve may cut after the festival, since the seven-day mitzva cancels the thirty-day decree.
Why does Abba Shaul speak of seven days, when the mishna says eight?
Abba Shaul holds part of a day counts as a whole, so the seventh day ends the seven days and begins the thirty.
Rav Ḥisda and Ravina bar Sheila rule the halakha follows Abba Shaul, and the Rabbis concede that cutting hair on Friday is allowed.
In accordance with whose opinion is Rav Amram's report of Rav's ruling on bathing?
Rav Amram cites Rav: once the comforters leave on the seventh day, the mourner may bathe.
It follows Abba Shaul, who treats part of the seventh day as a whole day.
Abaye rules the halakha follows Abba Shaul on the seventh day, and the Rabbis concede to him on the thirtieth day.
Rava disagrees on the seventh day, while the Neharde'a Sages apply Abba Shaul to both, citing Shmuel's principle to follow the lenient view.
From where do we derive the thirty-day mourning period?
A verbal analogy with pera for a nazirite, whose hair grows for thirty days, shows a mourner also grows hair for thirty days.
From where is it derived that a nazirite grows hair for thirty days?
Rav Mattana says an unspecified naziriteship lasts thirty days, since the word yihye has the numerical value of thirty.
Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua says all agree a mourner on the eve of a festival must wait until evening before bathing.
Rav Neḥemya son of Rav Yehoshua reports the same halakha, which Rav Pappi, Rav Pappa and Rav Huna were teaching together.
Does a festival that falls on the day of burial count toward the thirty-day mourning period, as Abaye asked Rava?
Rava replies that the festival does not count toward the thirty days.
Abaye objects from a baraita where a mourner counts five days after the festival, which suggests festival days were not counted.

20a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: General principle: mourning restrictions cut off by a festival stay prohibited, but public consolation continues during the festival.
If the burial was three days before a festival's end, the mourner counts seven days after, and the festival counts toward thirty.
Does the baraita's statement that the festival counts toward thirty days refer only to the latter clause, about burial during the festival?
Abaye objects to Rava from a baraita stating that the festival counts toward the thirty days even when burial was during it.
Ravin reports that Rabbi Yoḥanan held even burial during the festival counts toward the thirty days, and Rabbi Elazar ruled likewise.
A baraita on overturning the bed: Rabbi Eliezer requires three days before the festival, while the Rabbis require only one day or one hour.
Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon notes this is the old dispute between Beit Shammai, who say three days, and Beit Hillel, who say one day.
Rabbi Yoḥanan says one day or one hour, but Rava rules following the tanna of the mishna, who requires three days before the festival.
Ravina came to Sura, on the Euphrates.
Rav Ḥaviva asks Ravina what the halakha is on this issue.
Ravina replies: even one day, and even one hour.
Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba, Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Yitzḥak Nappaḥa were discussing where the seven-day mourning period is derived.
From where is the seven-day mourning period derived?
Amos 8:10 says turn your festivals into mourning, so mourning lasts seven days as a festival does.
Perhaps mourning is like Shavuot, which lasts only one day?
That derivation is needed for Reish Lakish, who learns from Shavuot that distant tidings bring one day of mourning.
A baraita: recent tidings bring seven and thirty days of mourning, distant tidings one day; Rabbi Akiva defines recent as within thirty days.
Rabba bar bar Ḥana cites Rabbi Yoḥanan: the halakha follows the majority, but here it follows Rabbi Akiva, the more lenient in mourning.
Rav Ḥisda and Rava rule that for distant tidings mourning lasts only one day, in the cases of Rav Ḥanina and Rav Natan bar Ami.
Rav Natan objects from a baraita that the one-day rule applies to five relatives, but parents require seven and thirty days.
Rava replies that Rav Natan's baraita is an individual opinion and is not the accepted halakha.
A baraita about Rabbi Tzadok, whose father died long before he learned of it, and the Elders' ruling, shows the opinion was held by few.
Is it really Rabbi Aḥiyya's view, given that Rav's father was Rabbi Ḥiyya's brother and Rav's own uncle asked a question?

20b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav evasively answers Rabbi Ḥiyya's questions about his mother and father, so Rabbi Ḥiyya realizes both siblings have died and removes his shoes.
The Gemara draws three lessons: mourners may not wear shoes, distant tidings bring one day of mourning, and part of a day counts as a whole.
Rabbi Ḥiyya and Rabbi Aḥiyya are two different people, so the apparent conflict dissolves.
Rabbi Yosei bar Avin and Rabbi Adda of Caesarea rule that recent tidings received during a festival or Shabbat become distant, so only one day of mourning applies.
Upon receiving belated news of a close relative's death, does one tear his garment or not?
Rabbi Mani says he does not tear, while Rabbi Ḥanina says he does tear.
Rabbi Mani challenges Rabbi Ḥanina: tearing without a seven-day mourning period would make no sense.
Is there really no tearing without a seven-day period of mourning?
A baraita says one who acquires a garment during the seven-day period must tear it, but not after it, suggesting tearing without mourning.
Rabbi Zeira explains the baraita: for a father or mother one tears even after seven days, as an honor, though generally tearing requires mourning.
A baraita lists the relatives a priest may not become impure for, yet for whom the mourner must mourn, including siblings and married sisters.
Rabbi Akiva says one also mourns with his relatives' close relatives; Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar and the Rabbis differ on the scope.
The Rabbis' view is identical to the first tanna's, so what is the difference between them?
The difference is whether one mourns with a relative only while in the same house, as Rav and Rav Huna instructed their sons.
Mar Ukva wanted to mourn for his brother-in-law, but Rav Huna said mourning is observed for a wife's in-laws only, not for other relatives.
A baraita states that when one's father-in-law or mother-in-law dies, the wife must mourn with the husband, not force her to paint or rouge.
Another baraita says the husband may not force her to beautify, but she may serve him wine and wash his feet, which appears to contradict the first.
Resolve it: the first baraita refers to in-laws, the second to other relatives.
A baraita confirms that mourning in honor of a wife applies only to her father-in-law and mother-in-law.
Ameimar tore his garment on his son's son's death, then tore again standing, after realizing he had torn sitting.
From where do we derive that tearing must be done while standing?
Job 1:20 says Job arose and tore his coat, so tearing is done standing.

21a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Ashi challenges: if rending requires standing, so should ḥalitza, yet a baraita allows sitting or reclining for ḥalitza.
Ḥalitza's verse does not say he will stand, whereas for rending the verse says Job arose.
Rami bar Ḥama derives from Job 1:20 that rending must be done while standing.
Perhaps Job did something beyond the requirement, since the same verse also says he shaved his head.
The halakha is instead derived from David's rending of his garments in II Samuel 13:31.
Perhaps David also went beyond the requirement, since the verse says he lay on the earth.
A baraita says sitting on a bed, chair, mortar or ground does not fulfill the mourning obligation to overturn the bed.
Rabbi Yoḥanan says one who did not overturn his bed did not fulfill the obligation, even if he lay on the ground.
Ameimar explains David was only as if on the ground, since he lowered his bed close to it.
A baraita lists activities a mourner is prohibited from, except teaching the public; Rabbi Yosei taught all day after his son died.
Rabba bar bar Ḥana, bereaved, considers not lecturing; Rabbi Ḥanina and Rav say he may lecture through a disseminator, not a meturgeman.
How then should he act so that he can be heard?
A baraita: Rabbi Yehuda bar Ilai whispered his lecture to Rabbi Ḥananya ben Akavya, who passed it to the public.
A baraita: Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua differ on when a mourner may don phylacteries and whether new visitors require removing them.
What is the reason of Rabbi Eliezer, as Rav Mattana asks?
Deuteronomy 34:8 and Amos 8:10 are cited to explain the two positions on the length of mourning.
But Rabbi Yehoshua also has Deuteronomy 34:8, so why does his view differ?
Moses was different, because his mourning was especially intense.
But Rabbi Eliezer also has the verse saying its end is as a bitter day, so why does he hold two days?
The main bitterness is one day, while the severity of mourning lasts two days.
Ulla rules the halakha follows Rabbi Eliezer on removing phylacteries and Rabbi Yehoshua on donning them.
According to Ulla, must a mourner who dons phylacteries on the second day remove them when new visitors come?
Ulla explicitly says one removes and redons phylacteries even a hundred times, and a baraita of Yehuda ben Teima agrees.
Rava says once one dons phylacteries he does not remove them, but Rava also rules like the mishna's tanna of three days.

21b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A mitzva is different: since putting on phylacteries is a mitzva, the mourner must do it even in the first three days.
A baraita: during the first three days a mourner may not work, but from then on may work privately at home, and a woman may spin at home.
A baraita: during the first three days a mourner may not visit another mourner's house to console, but later may sit with the mourners.
A baraita: during the first three days a mourner may not extend greetings, though he may respond; from the third to seventh day he may only respond.
Is a mourner really prohibited from extending greetings during the first three days?
A baraita on Rabbi Akiva's sons: Rabbi Akiva greeted the crowd on the first day, which suggests greeting is allowed.
Showing respect for the public is different; Rabbi Akiva was permitted to greet them as a courtesy.
The earlier baraita is restated: from the third to seventh day he may only respond, and afterward he resumes normal greetings.
Another baraita says a mourner may be consoled but not greeted during thirty days, which seems to contradict the first.
A baraita on a man who remarries within thirty days: he may not be consoled at home, implying the greeting prohibition lasts thirty days.
Rav Idi bar Avin reconciles: the first baraita is about the mourner, who may greet others after seven days, while others may not greet him.
The Gemara challenges: the baraita's permission to respond implies others may greet the mourner.
If the greeting was unknown to the mourner, why not allow response during the first three days too?
Another baraita on the twelve months: one may console but not greet during that period, and greet but not console after it.
Rabbi Meir compares consoling after twelve months to a physician who breaks a healed leg again, reopening the wound.
The twelve-month baraita concerns parents, and the seven-day baraita concerns other relatives.
Why not allow indirect consolation for other relatives after thirty days, as the baraita says no consolation at all?
A baraita on a mourner coming from nearby or far: whether he counts with the other mourners depends on the distance and the day.
Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba cites Rabbi Yoḥanan: the nearby mourner counts with the others only if the principal household member is present.
A dilemma is raised before the scholars.

22a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: If the principal household member went to the cemetery and stayed away, does a late mourner count with him or with the household?
Rabbi Yoḥanan says even if the principal member went to the cemetery, a mourner arriving counts with the household.
But a baraita says such a mourner counts seven days on his own.
Resolve it: counting with them applies if the principal member returned within three days, and counting alone if he did not.
Rava tells the people of Meḥoza that those who do not follow the coffin to the grave count from turning back at the city gates.
Rabbi Shimon says even a mourner arriving on the seventh day from nearby counts with the others.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi rules that this holds provided the consolers are still in the house when he arrives.
If the consolers have stirred to leave but have not yet left, is it as if they have left? The question stands unresolved.
A tradition: Rabbi Yoḥanan rules the halakha follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel on tereifa and Rabbi Shimon on mourning.
Mourning follows Rabbi Shimon as in the arriving mourner case, and the mucus-stopped intestine is kosher per Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.
What is this mucus?
Rav Kahana says it is the fat of the intestines that comes out under pressure.
A visitor travels to Eretz Yisrael to check the ruling with Rabbi Abba, who says the opposite on tereifa and asks whether the mourning view is accurate.
What about the ruling that the halakha follows Rabbi Shimon on mourning?
It is a dispute: Rav Ḥisda and Rabbi Yoḥanan hold the halakha follows Rabbi Shimon, while Rav Naḥman disagrees.
The conclusion: the halakha is not Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel on tereifa, but follows Rabbi Shimon on mourning, the lenient view.
A baraita: one may hasten a burial of other relatives but should prolong acute mourning for a parent, except on Shabbat or a festival eve.

22b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A baraita: for other relatives a mourner may reduce business and remove a shoulder garment optionally, but for parents he must do both.
A leading authority's father died; he wished to remove his garment, and a colleague refrained from doing so out of consideration.
Abaye says the first authority is Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and the colleague is Rabbi Ya'akov bar Aḥa, though others reverse them.
If the colleague was the leader, why did Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi refrain, since his own father Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel was Nasi?
A baraita on hair and celebrations: for parents one waits longer, cutting hair only when rebuked and entering joy only after twelve months.
Rabba bar bar Ḥana says the thirty-day rule covers only social gatherings, not weddings.
A baraita adds social gatherings after thirty days, which suggests the rule covers all celebrations; the Gemara calls this difficult.
Ameimar taught Rabba bar bar Ḥana's view as allowing immediate entry to a social gathering.
But a baraita says both celebrations and social gatherings require waiting thirty days.
The baraita concerns an initial gathering the mourner hosts, while Rabba bar bar Ḥana concerns a reciprocal one.
A baraita: for other relatives one rends a handbreadth, but for a parent he rends until his heart is revealed.
Rabbi Abbahu derives the handbreadth from II Samuel 1:11, since taking hold requires at least a handbreadth of cloth.
A baraita: for other relatives one rends only the outer garment, but for a parent one rends all garments.
Man and woman both rend; Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says a woman first rends the inner garment and turns it around.
For other relatives one may rend the hem or only the neck opening, but for a parent one must always rend the hem.
Rabbi Yehuda says a rent that does not separate the hem is a frivolous tear, not a mourning rend.
Rabbi Abbahu cites II Kings 2:12, which says he rent them in two pieces, to show the rend must appear as two pieces.
A baraita on tacking the tear: other relatives may be tacked after seven or thirty days, parents only after thirty; a woman may tack at once.
Ravin cites Rabbi Yoḥanan on how to rend: for parents one must rend by hand so as to ruin the garment.
Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba cites Rabbi Yoḥanan: rend the inner garment for others, the outer for parents; Rav Ḥisda extends this to a Nasi.
A baraita says the Nasi is compared to parents only for the rule on mending, so Rav Ḥisda's extension seems contradicted.
When the Nasi died, Rav Ḥisda told Rav Ḥanan bar Rava to stand on a mortar to show the rent to all.
For a Sage one removes the garment from the right shoulder, for a president of the court the left, and for a Nasi both.
A baraita on mourning customs: study halls stop for a Sage, a court president or a Nasi, and seating and Torah reading change accordingly.

23a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korḥa says mourners should sit silently at home, and Rabbi Ḥananya ben Gamliel's lecturing in a house of mourning is recalled.
A baraita sets out the weekly restrictions of mourning, and Rabbi Yehuda gives a different schedule for going out and sitting in synagogue.
A baraita: a mourner may not remarry for thirty days, and a widower may not marry another until three festivals have passed, per Rabbi Yehuda.
A mourner without children, or with young children, may marry immediately, for the sake of procreation or the children's care.
Yosef the Priest asked his late wife's sister to care for the children, and did not have relations with her for a long time.
What does the term a long time mean?
Rav Pappa says it means after thirty days.
A baraita on ironed garments: the Sages forbid during mourning ironed garments; Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon restrict them differently.
Abaye wore an old white garment following Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, while Rava wore a new red cloak following Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon.
The mishna teaches that Shabbat counts as a day of mourning without interrupting it, and Judea and Galilee differ on Shabbat mourning practice.

23b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Some hold there is some private mourning on Shabbat; others say there is none at all.
Those who say there is mourning rely on Shabbat counting as a day, and those who deny it rely on Shabbat not interrupting mourning.
If some mourning applied on Shabbat, teaching that it does not interrupt would be superfluous, so there must be none.
But the mishna teaches that Shabbat counts as a day of mourning, so some rites should apply?
The mishna mentions Shabbat counting only because it wants to teach that Festivals do not count, so the first clause is incidental.
For those who say there is mourning on Shabbat, why does the mishna say it does not interrupt the period?
That clause was included only because the mishna wanted to teach that Festivals interrupt mourning.
Is this a dispute between tannaim over whether some mourning rites apply on Shabbat?
A baraita on a mourner with a corpse laid out before him: he eats apart, and may not recline, eat meat, or drink wine.
A mourner may not recline, eat meat or drink wine, bless, or lead the Grace, and is exempt from Shema, prayer and mitzvot.
On Shabbat he reclines, eats meat and drinks wine, and is obligated in Shema, prayer and mitzvot; Rabban Gamliel adds all Shabbat mitzvot.
Rabbi Yoḥanan explains the practical difference: whether the mourner must have marital relations on Shabbat.
Is the dispute not whether there is some mourning on Shabbat with regard to private matters?
Perhaps the first tanna forbids relations only while the corpse lies before him, not after burial.
Alternatively, Rabban Gamliel permits relations only before mourning takes effect after burial, while after it he may forbid them.

24a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Yoḥanan asked Shmuel whether there is mourning on Shabbat, and Shmuel said there is none at all.
The Sages cite Shmuel that a mourner who has relations during mourning deserves death at the hand of Heaven.
Rav Pappa objects that the ruling only forbids relations, and is attributed to Rabbi Yoḥanan rather than Shmuel.
Shmuel derives from Leviticus 10:6 that a mourner who does not let his hair grow or rend his garments is liable to death.
Rafram bar Pappa cites Evel Rabbati that relations during mourning are forbidden, and a man who did so had his corpse dragged by pigs.
Shmuel's mnemonic lists which Shabbat mourning rites are obligatory (head uncovering, rending, bed) and which are optional (shoes, relations, washing).
Why would wearing shoes be optional on Shabbat, when uncovering the head is equally common and not a clear sign of mourning?
Shmuel's standard reasoning requires a special head wrapping, so uncovering the head openly displays mourning on Shabbat.
Rabbi Yoḥanan says the head covering may be removed on Shabbat only when the mourner has no shoes, since shoes reveal he is not observing mourning.
Shmuel says rending not at the time of death is not rending, yet great Sages were mourned and rent garments long after their deaths.
Those Sages are different, since their teachings are repeatedly mentioned, so each mention renews the grief.
Ravin cites Rav Amram's baraita that rending applies all seven days, which contradicts Shmuel's limit to the time of death.
That baraita concerns rending in honor of one's father or mother, which requires tearing a new garment even later.
Are the extra tears made for parents to be mended after mourning, and do the Sages disagree about this?
Rav Oshaya's father held that such tears may not be mended, and Rav Oshaya may have learned it from bar Kappara.
Rava permits walking in a torn robe at home on Shabbat, and Rav Yosef, citing Rabbi Yoḥanan, observes mourning at home even on Shabbat.
Mishna: Rabbi Eliezer says Shavuot is like Shabbat for mourning, Rabban Gamliel adds Rosh HaShana and Yom Kippur; Shmuel rules as Rabban Gamliel.
A baraita on an infant dying within thirty days: it is buried in arms, with one woman and two men, but not one man and two women.

24b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Abba Shaul permits one man and two women to carry out an infant, and no line of condolence or mourner's blessing is offered for it.
For a thirty-day-old infant, Rabbi Yehuda requires a coffin carried by two people, and then the line of condolence and blessings apply.
Rabbi Akiva says a one-year-old with the limbs of a two-year-old, or the reverse, is carried out on a bier like an adult.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar and Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya differ on whether the public must grieve for an infant.
Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda, citing Rabbi Yishmael, differ on the age at which poor and wealthy children are eulogized.
Rav Giddel cites Rav: the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda's ruling in the name of Rabbi Yishmael.
Rabbi Anani bar Sason teaches that a loss shortly before Shavuot counts the festival as seven days; Rabbi Ami rebukes him for presenting another's view.
Rabbi Yitzḥak Nappaḥa teaches the same Shavuot counting, and Rav Sheshet similarly rebukes him for not citing Rabbi Elazar.
Rabbi Elazar cites Rabbi Oshaya: Deuteronomy 16:16 shows Shavuot has seven days of redress like Passover, so it is a seven-day festival.
Rav Pappa and Ravina apply the same reckoning to Rosh HaShana and Sukkot, counting the festival days toward mourning.
Ravina came to Sura on the Euphrates.
Rav Ḥaviva asks whether Ravina ruled that the day before Rosh HaShana plus Rosh HaShana counts as fourteen days.
Ravina says it is reasonable according to Rabban Gamliel, who treats Rosh HaShana as a festival, but he did not rule so.
Mishna: mourners do not rend or remove garments on festival intermediate days, and consolers offer the first meal only on an upright bed.

25a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Is the mishna's limit to relatives valid even for a Torah Sage, given a baraita saying everyone is his relative?
Everyone is like a relative only in the sense of rending and mourning; the mishna concerns a non-scholar.
If the deceased was an upright person, should all present rend garments, given a baraita about children dying so the father will mourn?
The baraita means the children died because the father failed to mourn an upright person; the mishna concerns a non-upright person.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says whoever stands by the dying person must rend, which conflicts with the mishna's limit.
The mishna refers to one who was not present at death and heard of the death of a non-relative who was neither scholar nor upright.
When Rav Safra died, the Sages did not rend garments; Abaye rebukes them, since a Torah scholar's death obliges rending.
Abaye adds that rending is owed while the scholar is eulogized, but the honor is at the eulogy, so they should wait.
When Rav Huna died, Rav Ḥisda refused to place a Torah scroll on his bier, since Rav Huna did not sit with one on his bed.
They could not fit the bier through the door, and Rav Ḥisda says a scholar's honor is to be taken out through the main opening.
Rav Ḥisda says a scholar's honor is to be carried on the first bier, and they broke the doorway to take him out.
Rav Yehuda cites II Samuel 6:3, that the Ark was placed on a new cart, to show a scholar's honor is on the first bier.
Rabbi Abba's eulogy says the Divine Presence would have rested on Rav Huna except that Babylonia prevented it.
Rav Naḥman bar Ḥisda objects from Ezekiel 1:3, which shows prophecy outside Eretz Yisrael.
The doubled word hayo haya implies Ezekiel had already begun prophesying in Eretz Yisrael.
Rav Huna's funeral arrives in Eretz Yisrael, and Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi, mistaking the news, say they could not lift their heads before him.
Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi go out to meet the funeral, while Rabbi Ila and Rabbi Ḥanina do not.
Why did those who went out do so, and why did the others not, given conflicting baraitot on standing in line for a passing coffin?
If the baraitot conflict, how do they reconcile?
They differ on whether the skeleton is intact; Rav Huna's was intact, and the other Sage was not assured of that.
The Sages of Eretz Yisrael decide to bury Rav Huna next to Rabbi Ḥiyya, since both disseminated Torah.
Who will take him into Rabbi Ḥiyya's burial cave, since few are fit to enter?
Rav Ḥagga says he will, having studied before Rabbi Ḥiyya from age eighteen and seen his scrupulous conduct.
Rav Ḥagga takes him in; Ḥizkiyya's corpse rises beside a pillar of fire, and Rav Ḥagga sets the coffin as a protection and is not harmed.
When Rav Ḥisda died, Rabbi Yitzḥak objects to placing a Torah scroll on his bier, since he did not hold that during life.
Rabbi Yitzḥak bar Ami rules that the tears of a Torah Sage may be tacked once they turn their faces from the bier.
Rabba bar Huna and Rav Hamnuna are both taken up to Eretz Yisrael for burial.

25b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: When the two Sages reached the bridge their camels stopped moving.
A passing Arab asks what this stopping of the camels means.
The Sages explain that they are showing honor to each other, each urging the other to cross first.
The Arab rules that by law Rabba bar Huna should go first as the son of a great man.
The camel of Rabba bar Huna then crosses first.
Shortly afterwards the Arab's molars and teeth fell out as punishment for his disrespect.
A child recites a eulogy for Rabba bar Rav Huna, describing his greatness and his soul's reward.
When Ravina died, a eulogizer opened his eulogy for him.
The eulogy compares Ravina to a date-palm and calls for nights of weeping like days of study.
Rav Ashi asks bar Kippok what he will say in his eulogy on the day Ravina dies.
Bar Kippok answers with a eulogy built on images of cedars, hyssop, leviathan, fish and rivers.
Bar Avin objects that comparing the righteous to hook and flame is wrong, since these are not honorific.
Rav Ashi asks what bar Kippok will say instead.
Bar Kippok offers a better eulogy: weep for the mourners, since the departed has gone to rest.
Rav Ashi was offended, and as a result the two eulogists' feet turned crooked.
On the day Ravina died neither of them came to eulogize him.
Rav Ashi's saying: neither bar Kippok nor bar Avin can perform halitza because their feet are crooked.
Rava, fearing the Tigris, asks bar Avin to rise and pray on his behalf.
Bar Avin prays, asking for mercy and not to be punished like the bitter water.
A parenthetical mnemonic list of the names of the eulogized sages that follow.
Rabbi Ḥanin, a son-in-law of the Nasi, had no children until he prayed and then had a son.
On the day his son was born, Rabbi Ḥanin died and a eulogizer opened his eulogy.
The eulogy describes joy turned to sorrow and the grace of the newborn lost with his father.
They named the child Ḥanan after his father, and then Rabbi Ḥanin died.
When Rabbi Yoḥanan died, Rabbi Yitzḥak ben Elazar opened his eulogy.
The eulogy says that the loss of Rabbi Yoḥanan is as hard for Israel as a sun setting at noon.
The eulogy supports this with the verse from Amos about the sun going down at noon.
Rabbi Yoḥanan asserts that the verse refers to the day King Josiah was killed.
When Rabbi Yoḥanan died, the sages recorded how Rabbi Ami reacted.
Rabbi Ami sat in mourning for thirty days, seven days and thirty days.
Rabbi Abba holds that Rabbi Ami's mourning practice was his own choice and not normative.
Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba cites Rabbi Yoḥanan as the source for this view.
Rabbi Yoḥanan rules that even for a teacher who taught wisdom one mourns only one day.
When Rabbi Zeira died, a eulogizer opened his eulogy for him.
The eulogy says Babylon bore Rabbi Zeira and the Land of Israel raised him, and Tiberias mourns his loss.
When Rabbi Abbahu died, the pillars of his city Caesarea ran with water like tears.
When Rabbi Yosei died, the gutters of his city Tzippori flowed with blood.
When Rabbi Ya'akov died, stars appeared in the daytime.
When Rabbi Asi died, all the trees were uprooted.
When Rabbi Ḥiyya died, fiery stones fell from the sky.
When Rabbi Menaḥem died, the statues' faces became smooth like plastered walls.
When Rabbi Tanḥum bar Ḥiyya died, the royal statues were mutilated.
When Rabbi Elyashiv died, seventy thieves' tunnels were dug in Neharde'a, since he had prevented theft.
When Rav Hamnuna died, hailstones fell from the sky.
When Rabba and Rav Yosef died, the bridge arches of the Euphrates collapsed toward each other.
When Abaye and Rava died, the bridge arches of the Tigris collapsed toward each other.
When Rabbi Mesharshiyya died, the palm trees became laden with thorns.
The Sages taught a baraita, introducing the next topic of tearing garments in mourning.

26a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A baraita lists the mourning rents that can never be mended: for parents, teacher, Nasi, court head, bad news, Torah scroll, and the ruined cities, Temple and Jerusalem.
The baraita gives the order for mourning Jerusalem: first rend for the Temple, then extend the rent for Jerusalem.
The Gemara asks from where we derive rending garments for parents and teacher.
Elisha's cry over Elijah, my father, my father, chariots of Israel, supports rending for parents and teacher.
The Gemara asks what basis there is for reading the teacher into the verse.
Rav Yosef's translation renders the verse as referring to a teacher who protected Israel better than chariots.
The Gemara asks from where we know that such rents are never properly mended.
The verse says Elisha tore his clothes in two, and the phrase in two shows the rents stay torn forever.
Reish Lakish asks Rabbi Yoḥanan why Elisha mourned while Elijah is still alive.
Since the verse says he saw him no more, Elijah was treated as dead from Elisha's perspective.
The Gemara asks from where the rule for the Nasi, court head and evil tidings is derived.
David rent his clothes over Saul, Jonathan, the people of the Lord and the house of Israel fallen by the sword.
The verse's terms are matched: Saul is the Nasi, Jonathan the court head, and the people and house are evil tidings.
Rav bar Shaba objects that rending may be required only when all these calamities happen together.
The repeated word for divides the matter, so each misfortune alone is sufficient cause to rend.
The Gemara asks whether we really rend garments upon hearing evil tidings.
Shmuel did not rend garments when Shapur killed twelve thousand Jews, which seems to contradict the rule.
Rending is required only for a calamity affecting the majority of the people, like the defeat under Saul.
The Gemara asks whether Shapur really killed Jews at all.
Shapur told Shmuel he had never killed a Jew, so the claim seems inaccurate.
Shapur never instigated the killings; the people brought them on themselves by rebelling against him.
The Gemara asks from where we derive rending garments upon hearing God's name cursed.
Eliakim, Shebna and Joah came to Hezekiah with their clothes rent after Rab-shakeh's blasphemy.
A baraita rules that hearers must rend, but the witnesses need not, since they already rent when they first heard.
The Gemara asks what difference the first hearing makes, since they heard the curse again now.
That cannot be the case, as the verse shows the king rent his garments but the messengers did not.
Hezekiah rent his clothes when he heard, while those who reported did not rend theirs again.
The Gemara asks from where we derive that such rents may not be properly mended.
A verbal analogy between the word rending in the case of Hezekiah and that of Elijah and Elisha.
The Gemara asks from where we derive rending garments when a Torah scroll is burned.
Jehudi cut Jeremiah's scroll with a penknife and burned it, which shows the scroll-burning case.
The Gemara asks what the three or four leaves mean and why he cut the scroll only at that point.
They told Jehoiakim that Jeremiah had written a book of Lamentations about Jerusalem's future destruction.
Jehoiakim asks what is written in the book.
They read him the first verse of Lamentations, How does the city sit solitary.
Jehoiakim rejects it, saying he is the king and it does not apply to him.
They read him the second verse, She weeps sore in the night.
Jehoiakim again answers that he is the king and the verse does not apply to him.
They read the third verse, Judah is gone into exile because of affliction.
Jehoiakim replies once more that he is the king.
They read the fourth verse, The ways of Zion do mourn.
Jehoiakim repeats that he is the king and it does not apply to him.
They read the fifth verse, Her adversaries have become the chief, foretelling the king's removal.
Jehoiakim asks who said this.
They tell him it continues: the Lord has afflicted her for the multitude of her transgressions.
He immediately cut out all the divine names from the book and burned them in the fire.
The verse says they were not afraid nor rent their garments, which implies they should have rent.
By inference, they were required to rend their garments when they saw the burning.
Rav Pappa suggests the rending was due to evil tidings in the scroll, not the scroll's destruction.
Abaye replies that these were not evil tidings at that time, but a prophecy, not current events.
Rav Huna rules that one who sees a torn Torah scroll rends twice, once for the parchment and once for the writing.
The verse says after the king burned the scroll and the words, which implies separate rents for each.
Rabbi Abba sat with Rav Huna bar Ḥiyya, and an ostrich tried to swallow Rabbi Abba's phylacteries.
Rabbi Abba says that had it swallowed them, he would be obligated to make two rents.
Rav Huna asks Rabbi Abba from where he derives this.
Rabbi Abba recounts that he asked Rav Mattana, who had no answer, then asked Rav Yehuda.
Shmuel taught through Rav Yehuda that rending is required only when a sacred book is torn by force, like Jehoiakim's case.
The Gemara asks from where we derive rending garments upon seeing the cities of Judea in ruin.
The verse about men from Shechem, Shiloh and Samaria with rent clothes shows rending at seeing the destruction.
Rabbi Ḥelbo, citing Ulla Bira'a, states the rule that one rends at seeing the ruin in awe.
Rabbi Elazar says one who sees the cities of Judea in ruin recites Your sacred cities are a wilderness, then rends.
One who sees Jerusalem in ruin recites Zion is a wilderness and Jerusalem a desolation, then rends.
One who sees the Temple in ruin recites the verse about our burned house, then rends.
The baraita's conclusion: one rends for the Temple and extends the rent for Jerusalem.
A contradicting baraita says one rends separately for the Temple and for Jerusalem once reaching Scopus.
The baraita is not contradictory: each refers to which site one reached first on the approach.
A baraita permits tacking, hemming and gathering the rents, but not mending them with precise stitches.
Rav Ḥisda says the following, introducing the next teaching.

26b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Explains that the reference is to the Alexandrian method of mending, which leaves no visible tear.
Introduces a baraita.
A baraita rules that rending in a loosely tacked or ladder-stitched place does not fulfil the obligation, but rending a carefully mended place does.
Rav Ḥisda says the Alexandrian mending in the baraita is ordinary-quality sewing rather than ordinary mending.
Introduces another baraita about the Alexandrian mending.
One may turn a garment rent at the top upside down and then mend it carefully.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar prohibits careful mending even in that case.
The seller is forbidden to mend, so the buyer is too, and the seller must inform the buyer.
Rabbi Meir: the initial rending is a handbreadth, and the extension is three fingerbreadths.
Rabbi Yehuda: the initial rending is three fingerbreadths, and the extension may be any amount.
Ulla rules like Rabbi Meir on the initial rending and like Rabbi Yehuda on the extension.
A baraita states Rabbi Yosei's view: a handbreadth initially and any minimal amount for the extension.
If told first of father's death then son's, the lower part of the rent for the son may be mended, but not the upper part for the father.
If told first of son's death then father's, the upper part for the son may be mended but not the lower part for the father.
If told of several deaths at once, one rent may cover all of them.
Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira holds one rent for all other relatives and a separate rent for father and mother, since one cannot add to that rent.
The Gemara asks the reason for Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira's view that one may not add to the parents' rent.
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak: one has only one father and one mother, so they cannot be added to.
Shmuel rules that the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira.
The Gemara asks whether Shmuel really said this, given his principle about lenient rulings in mourning.
Shmuel's own principle favors the lenient view, which contradicts ruling stringently here.
A baraita states how far one may rend: to the navel, with some saying to the heart.
Although there is no direct proof, the verse rend your hearts and not your garments alludes to the heart limit.
Once the rent reaches the navel, one moves three fingerbreadths away and rends anew, turning the garment if needed.
If the garment is full of rents above, one turns it bottom to top and rends the bottom.
Rending at the bottom or sides does not discharge the obligation, except the High Priest may rend at the bottom.
Rav Mattana and Mar Ukva report disagreeing traditions attributed to Shmuel's father and Levi.
One view: within the first seven days a new rent is made for each new death, then only an extension.
The other view: within the first thirty days a new rent is made for each new death, then only an extension.
Rabbi Zeira objects: why not simply extend the first rent during the seven days, given the rule about tacking.
The Master taught that a woman may tack her rent immediately, which Rabbi Zeira cites as a comparison.
There it is due to the woman's honor, since a torn garment would be embarrassing, but the rent still counts as existing.
Rabbi Zeira asks why the thirty-day view does not allow extending the parents' rent, which is never mended.
There the son may not mend it due to honor for his parents, but the tear is treated as sewn up, so he may extend it.
A baraita says one who goes out in a torn garment before the dead, from an earlier bereavement, steals from the dead and the living.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel: one who borrows a cloak to visit a sick father, and finds him dead, may tear it.
He then returns the cloak with payment for the depreciation, and if he did not warn the lender, he must not touch it.
A baraita: the sick person's relatives are not told of a death, and women are silenced so he does not learn of it.
Garments of minors are rent to arouse grief, and one rends for in-laws out of honor for his wife.
Rav Pappa says a mourner should not hold a young child in his lap, lest the child cause him to laugh.
Consolers do not provide the meal of comfort on overturned beds.
A baraita: a visitor of close friendship sits with the mourner on overturned beds, otherwise both sit on upright beds.
Rava's relative died and Abba bar Marta came to visit, but overturned the bed as if they were close friends.
Rava stood the bed upright, treating Abba bar Marta as an ordinary visitor.
Rava reproaches the scholar for lacking sense, since he had shown he was not considered a close friend.
A baraita on one who learns of a close relative's death while traveling from place to place.

27a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A mourner whose business is affected may reduce his business if possible, otherwise he may carry on with partners.
A baraita: mourners overturn their beds from when the corpse leaves the house, per Rabbi Eliezer, or from when the grave is sealed, per Rabbi Yehoshua.
The Nasi Rabban Gamliel the Elder died, and Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua gave different times to overturn beds, which were already overturned.
A baraita: on Shabbat eve the beds are stood upright from minḥa time onward.
Rabba bar Huna adds that one may not sit on the upright bed until dark, and after Shabbat one must overturn the bed again.
A baraita: the mourner must overturn every bed in his house, even in ten places or among five brothers.
Beds used only for storing garments need not be overturned, and a dargash is stood upright rather than overturned.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel: for a dargash one loosens its loops so that it falls on its own.
The Gemara asks what a dargash is.
Ulla explains it is a gada, an ornamental bed kept for good luck and not used for sleeping.
Rabba objects that the mourner king reclines on a dargash at the mourner's meal, which would be a new honor during mourning.
Rav Ashi objects to Rabba's difficulty and asks what it actually is.
Rav Ashi answers that the case is like food and drink: the mourner is served now only because he is a mourner.
The Gemara restates the difficulty against the mishna that says all beds, including the good-luck bed, must be overturned.
A baraita: a dargash need not be overturned but only stood upright.
The Gemara asks why a good-luck bed need not be overturned, given the mishna's rule.
The mishna states that the mourner overturns all the beds in his house.
The Gemara asks what the difficulty is.
A bed used for garments is exempt, so a dargash, being a non-sleeping bed, is exempt too.
The Gemara restates the difficulty from Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's view that the dargash loops fall on their own.
If a dargash were a good-luck bed like other beds, it would have no loops at all.
When Ravin came from Eretz Yisrael to Babylonia, Rav Taḥalifa was asked about the dargash.
Ravin asks what a dargash is.
Rav Taḥalifa answers that a dargash is a leather bed.
Rabbi Yirmeya explains that a dargash has its interlacing from within, so its loops fall out, unlike a bed.
Rabbi Ya'akov bar Aḥa, citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, rules that the halakha follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel on a dargash.
Rabbi Ya'akov bar Aḥa, citing Rabbi Asi, says a bed with long posts may simply be stood upright.
A baraita: a mourner who sleeps on a chair, a mortar or the ground does not fulfil the obligation.
Rabbi Yoḥanan explains the reason: he did not fulfil the mitzva of overturning the bed.
A baraita permits sweeping, sprinkling and washing vessels in the mourner's house but forbids bringing incense or spices.
The Gemara asks: but Bar Kappara taught that one may not bless over incense or spices in the mourner's house, implying they may be brought.
The baraitot differ in place: the mourner's house versus the house of the consolers, where spices may be brought.
Mishna: the first meal after the burial is not brought in a tray, bowl or narrow basket, and mourners' blessings are not recited on the intermediate days of a Festival.
Mishna: a bier is not set down in the street during the intermediate Festival days, and women's biers are never set down, out of honor.
A baraita: the rich used silver and gold baskets while the poor used willow baskets, so the Sages made all use willow for the poor's honor.
A baraita: the rich used white glass cups and the poor colored ones, so all were made to use colored glass for the poor's honor.
A baraita: the faces of the rich were uncovered and the poor's covered, so the Sages ruled all faces be covered for the poor's honor.
A baraita: the rich were carried out to burial on a dargash while the poor were carried out differently, which the text continues.

27b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Continuing the history: everyone is taken out on a plain bier, out of honor for the poor.
Incense was once placed under all who died of intestinal disease, out of honor for the living sufferers.
Utensils used by dying menstruants and zavin were once all immersed, and the Sages extended this to all dying women and men for their honor.
Burial was once costly, so Rabban Gamliel asked to be buried in linen and the people followed him.
Rav Pappa notes that nowadays everyone is buried even in plain hemp garments costing a dinar.
A bier is not set down in the street, as the mishna teaches.
Rav Pappa rules there is no festival restriction on eulogizing a Torah scholar in his presence, and all the more so on Hanukkah and Purim.
The Gemara objects: Rav Kahana eulogized Rav Zevid during a festival, which seems to contradict the ruling.
Rav Pappi explains that it was the day the news arrived, and a eulogy then counts as if in his presence.
Ulla says hesped literally means striking oneself on the heart.
The verse about striking the breasts supports Ulla's meaning of hesped.
Tipuaḥ means clapping hands together and killus means stomping the foot.
A baraita: one who stomps in mourning should wear a shoe, not a sandal, to avoid injury.
Rabbi Yoḥanan rules that once a mourner nods his head, the consolers may no longer sit beside him.
Rabbi Yoḥanan rules that everyone must stand before the Nasi except a mourner and one who is sick.
Rabbi Yoḥanan adds that one tells everyone to be seated, except a mourner and one who is sick.
Rav Yehuda, citing Rav, rules that a mourner on the first day may not eat his own bread.
The verse nor eat the bread of men, said to Ezekiel, supports the ruling that mourners eat others' bread.
Rabba and Rav Yosef, while mourning, exchanged meals with each other.
Rav Yehuda, citing Rav, rules that when a person dies in a city, all residents may not work until burial.
Rav Hamnuna hears a shofar announcing a death in Darumata, sees people working, and excommunicates them.
They reply that each group in the town is responsible for its own dead, and theirs was not the deceased.
Rav Hamnuna accepts this, saying they are permitted, and revokes his excommunication.
Rav Yehuda, citing Rav, rules that one who grieves excessively over his dead will in the end weep for another.
A woman near Rav Huna lost seven sons and wept excessively over the first, as the rule predicted.
Rav Huna warned her not to continue, and she ignored him.
He warned that she should heed him or prepare shrouds for another death, and all her sons died.
He told her to prepare her own shrouds, and soon she died.
The verse Weep not for the dead nor bemoan him is cited to set limits on excessive mourning.
The Gemara asks what the appropriate measure of mourning is and how it works.
Three days of weeping, seven of eulogy, and thirty for ironing and cutting hair, after which the mourning period ends.
God says: do not be more merciful with the dead than I am; the Torah's prescribed mourning suffices.
The verse Weep sore for him that goes away is cited about extended mourning.
Rav Yehuda says that the verse refers to one who dies without children, for whom mourning is more intense.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi would go to a mourning house only for one who died without children.
The verse says he shall return no more nor see his native land, which Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi uses for his practice.
Rav Huna reads the verse differently: the one who goes is someone who sins and repeats the sin.
Rav Huna applies his standard reasoning: once a person sins and repeats it, it becomes permitted to him.
The Gemara objects that the wording is wrong and must be restated as it becomes like something permitted.
Rabbi Levi rules that in the first three days a mourner sees a sword lying between his thighs.
From the third to the seventh day the sword lies opposite him in the corner.
After seven days the sword moves before him in the marketplace, and the fear is less.
Mishna: the bier of a woman is never set down, out of honor.
The Sages of Neharde'a say that this ruling was taught only for the case described.

28a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Only a woman who died in childbirth is exempt; the biers of other women may be set down in the street.
Rabbi Elazar says even the biers of other women may not be set down in the street.
Miriam died and was buried there, showing burial should be close to the place of death.
Rabbi Elazar adds that Miriam, like Moses, died by the divine kiss.
A verbal analogy with there in the verse about Moses shows her death was by a divine kiss, left unstated out of decency.
Rabbi Ami explains the juxtaposition of Miriam's death with the red heifer: the righteous' death atones like the heifer.
Rabbi Elazar explains the juxtaposition of Aaron's death with the priestly garments: the death of the righteous atones.
A baraita defines sudden death, an expedited death after a day of illness, and related categories.
Rabbi Ḥananya ben Gamliel says a death from a plague is a death at a stroke.
Ezekiel's verses about the sudden loss of his wife at a stroke and her death that evening support this classification.
The baraita continues: two days of sickness is quickened death, and five days of sickness is the ordinary death of all people.
Rabbi Ḥanin is asked what verse supports this scheme.
Deuteronomy's behold your days approach is expounded in parts, with hen meaning one in Greek, totaling five.
Death at fifty is karet, at fifty-two is the death of Samuel from Ramah, and at sixty is death by Heaven.
Mar Zutra states that a death at sixty is a death by Heaven.
Mar Zutra is asked what verse supports this.
Job's phrase in a ripe age, bekhelaḥ, has numerical value sixty, alluding to a divine punishment.
Death at seventy is old age, and at eighty is death in strength.
Psalms' seventy years and eighty by reason of strength supports these ages.
Rabba says death from fifty to sixty is also karet, and the sages did not count it due to the honor of Samuel.
The sages did not count it because Samuel of Ramah died at fifty-two, out of his honor.
When Rav Yosef turned sixty he made a holiday for the Sages.
Rav Yosef explains that he has passed the age of karet.
Abaye asks whether Rav Yosef escaped the karet of days, meaning sudden death.
Rav Yosef replies that he should at least grasp half, since he escaped one type of karet.
Rav Huna died suddenly, and the Sages feared it was a bad sign.
Zuga of Hadayeiv explains these principles apply only before the age of strength, eighty.
Sudden death after reaching the age of strength is death by a divine kiss.
Rava says length of life, children and sustenance depend on fate, not merit.
Rabba and Rav Ḥisda were both pious, yet rain came to each through prayer, showing fate's role.
Rav Ḥisda lived ninety-two years and had sixty wedding feasts, while Rabba lived forty and had sixty calamities.
Rav Ḥisda's house had fine bread even for dogs, while Rabba's had coarse barley bread for people.
Rava says he received Rav Huna's wisdom and Rav Ḥisda's wealth but not Rabba bar Rav Huna's humility.
Rav Seorim, Rava's brother, sat before Rava and saw he was dozing toward death.
Rava asks Rav Seorim to tell the Angel of Death not to torment him.
Rav Seorim asks whether Rava is not the Angel of Death's friend.
Rava replies that since his fate was handed over and death decreed, the Angel no longer heeds him.
Rava is asked to appear in a dream after death, and he does.
Asked about pain in death, Rava says it was like the prick of a knife when letting blood.
Rava sat before Rav Naḥman, who saw him dozing and asked Rava to tell the Angel not to torment him.
Rava asks whether Rav Naḥman is not an important person in Heaven.
Rav Naḥman replies that in the supernal world no one is important, honorable or complete.
Rava asks Rav Naḥman to appear to him in a dream after death.
Asked about pain, Rav Naḥman says it was like removing hair from milk, very gentle.
Rav Naḥman says he would not want to return to the world, since the fear of the Angel of Death is great.
The Angel of Death appeared to Rabbi Elazar while he was eating teruma.
Rabbi Elazar argued that teruma is sacred, so dying now would defile it, and the Angel left him.
The Angel appeared to Rav Sheshet in the market; he asked to die at home like a human, not in the market like an animal.
Rav Ashi asks the Angel of Death for thirty days to review his studies.
On the thirtieth day the Angel came to take Rav Ashi.
Rav Ashi asks why the Angel is in such a hurry and cannot postpone his death.
The Angel replies that Rav Huna bar Natan is pressing to succeed him, and two kingdoms cannot overlap at all.
The Angel could not take Rav Ḥisda, whose mouth never stopped studying, until a cedar column cracked and startled him into silence.
The Angel could not approach Rabbi Ḥiyya because of his righteousness, so he came disguised as a poor man at his door.
The disguised Angel asked Rabbi Ḥiyya for bread, and he gave it.
The Angel appealed to him to show mercy to a poor man, as he sought his life.
The Angel revealed himself with a fiery rod, and Rabbi Ḥiyya surrendered his soul.
