ranges.en: Mishnah rule: women may wail but not clap on festival intermediate days.
Rabbi Yishmael's view: those close to the bier may clap.
On New Moons, Hanukkah and Purim both wailing and clapping are allowed; after burial neither.
Explains wailing as all crying together and lament as one leading while the rest respond.
Jeremiah's verse telling daughters to learn wailing and lament supports the definition.
Isaiah's promise that God will destroy death forever frames mourning with a hopeful future.
Asks what the mourning women actually say.
Rav's formula: woe over the one departing, woe over the returning pledge.
Rava reports the Shekhantziv women's formula using the same wording.
Shekhantziv saying: a bone removed from the jaw and water returns to the kettle.
Shekhantziv saying: wrap the mountains in mourning since the dead was of high rank.
Shekhantziv saying: lend a fine cloak as shroud for one who lost his fortune.
Shekhantziv saying: a person runs and tumbles at the ford yet still borrows.
Shekhantziv saying: merchants will be examined to see whether they are honest.
Shekhantziv saying: death is like death, and suffering is like interest.
Introduces a baraita attributed to Rabbi Meir.
Ecclesiastes verse on going to a house of mourning supports Rabbi Meir's teaching.
Explains that the matters the living should take to heart are matters of death.
Rabbi Meir's list: those who eulogize, bury, or praise at length receive the same treatment.
Alternative teaching: one who does not raise his voice in weeping gets no one weeping for him.
Proverbs verse about being called up higher supports the teaching on humility.
Introduces four elders who came to console Rabbi Yishmael after his sons died.
Rabbi Tarfon instructs that each should speak something new without interrupting another.
Rabbi Akiva says he will speak last.
Rabbi Yishmael attributes his repeated bereavements to his own sins.
Introduces Rabbi Tarfon's response.
Leviticus verse calling the whole house of Israel to bewail the burning.
A fortiori: Nadav and Avihu merited mourning for one mitzva, so Yishmael's sons deserve more.
Introduces Rabbi Yosei HaGelili's response.
Kings verse that all Israel shall mourn and bury Abijah supports his argument.
A fortiori from Abijah, who did one good thing, to the sons of Rabbi Yishmael.
Asks what the one good deed of Abijah was; names two disputing Sages.
First view: Abijah abandoned his guard duty and went up to Jerusalem for the festival.
Second view: Abijah removed the guard posts his father placed on the roads.
Introduces Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya's response.
Jeremiah verse on Zedekiah dying in peace, with a fortiori argument to Yishmael's sons.
Introduces Rabbi Akiva's response.
Zechariah verse: great mourning in Jerusalem like the mourning of Hadadrimmon.
Rav Yosef says he would not understand this verse without its Aramaic translation.
The Aramaic translation compares that mourning to the mourning for Ahab and Josiah.
A fortiori from Ahab, who did one good thing, to the sons of Rabbi Yishmael.
Rava objects: Zedekiah is said to die in peace yet had his eyes put out.
Rabba bar Mari answers that Nebuchadnezzar died in Zedekiah's lifetime.
Rava objects: Josiah is said to be gathered in peace yet was shot by archers.
Rav Yehuda, citing Rav, says the arrows made Josiah's body like a sieve.
Rabba bar Mari answers that the Temple was not destroyed in Josiah's lifetime.
Rabbi Yochanan rules that consolers may not speak until the mourner opens his mouth.
Job's verse: after Job opened his mouth, Eliphaz the Temanite answered.
Rabbi Abbahu states that a mourner reclines at the head of the table and seeks its source.
Job verse: he sat as chief and comforted mourners, supporting the mourner's seat.
Objection: yenaḥem means he comforts others, so the verse refers to the comforter.
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak: the word is written yinaḥem, meaning will be comforted, the mourner.
Mar Zutra's Amos verse proof: the bitter mourner is made prince over those who comfort him.
Rabbi Chama bar Chanina asks the source for a groom reclining at the head of the table.
Isaiah verse: as a priest is at the head, so a groom reclines at the head.
The Gemara asks from where we learn that the priest himself sits at the head.
School of Rabbi Yishmael: from Leviticus, sanctify him in all matters of sanctity, including first place.
Rabbi Chanina states that the soul's departure from the body is difficult.

ranges.en: Simile: passing a knotted rope through a rigging eye is as hard as a halyard passing through one.
Rabbi Levi bar Chiyta: to one leaving the dead say go in peace; to one leaving the living say go to peace.
Restates the rule for one leaving the dead: say go in peace, not go to peace.
Genesis verse that you shall go to your fathers in peace supports the rule for the dead.
Restates the rule for one leaving the living: say go to peace, not go in peace.
Examples: David told Absalom go in peace and he was hanged; Jethro told Moses go to peace and he prospered.
Rabbi Levi: one who moves from synagogue to study hall or back merits receiving the Divine Presence.
Psalms verse: they go from strength to strength and appear before God in Zion supports Rabbi Levi.
Rav Chiyya bar Ashi, citing Rav: Torah scholars have no rest, even in the World-to-Come.
Psalms verse of constant movement from strength to strength is cited to support Rav's statement.
Closing formula of the tractate Moed Katan (Hadran).
